passages.title: Revelation from the Lord before whom heavens tremble
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat open Sūrah ash-Shūrā by placing the Qur'an in its true setting: it is not an isolated or unprecedented thing, but revelation sent down to the Prophet ﷺ just as Books and Scriptures were sent to the prophets before him — by a Lord who owns everything in the heavens and the earth, whose heavens are on the verge of bursting apart, and whose angels fill them with praise and with pleading for the people of the earth. The passage moves in one continuous line: from **revelation**, to **the One who reveals**, to **the state of creation above us**, and finally to **those who turn away from Him anyway** — and what the Prophet ﷺ is, and is not, responsible for regarding them.

## The letters that open the sūrah: Ḥā Mīm, ʿAyn Sīn Qāf

The sūrah begins with two lines of detached Arabic letters. Ibn Kathir does not offer a new interpretation here; he simply refers back to his earlier discussion of these letters. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is blunt and beautiful about it: **only Allah knows the meaning of these letters.**

That is not a dodge; it is the right posture for opening a passage about revelation. The very first thing the reader meets is something he cannot decode on his own — a reminder, before a single argument is made, that this Book comes from above his own reach, and that reverent silence before what Allah has not disclosed is itself a form of faith.

## Revelation: the same Lord, the same act

"Likewise Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise sends revelation to you as to those before you."

Ibn Kathir gives the sense plainly: *just as this Qur'an has been revealed to you, so too the Books and Scriptures were revealed to the Prophets who came before you.* The Prophet ﷺ stands in a line. The same Lord, the same kind of act, stretching back through the prophets who preceded him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the purpose behind it: this sūrah was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ **for the ascertainment of the religious principles and for other benefits** — revelation is not decoration, it is how the foundations of religion are fixed and known.

Then two of Allah's names close the ayah, and they are chosen with care:

- **al-ʿAzīz** — rendered "the Almighty". Ibn Kathir specifies the sense operating here: almighty **in His vengeance**.
- **al-Ḥakīm** — "the All-Wise". Ibn Kathir: wise **in all that He says and does**. Not only His acts but His speech — including the very words being revealed — issue from perfect wisdom.

Set together, the pair says: the One sending this Book is not to be trifled with, and nothing in it is arbitrary.

## How the revelation came to him ﷺ

Right at this point Ibn Kathir gives us a window into the lived experience of revelation. Imam Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, narrated that ʿĀ'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said that al-Ḥārith bin Hishām asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, "O Messenger of Allah, how does the revelation come to you?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Sometimes it comes to me like the ringing of a bell, which is the most difficult for me; then it goes away, and I understand what was said. And sometimes the angel comes to me in the image of a man, and he speaks to me and I understand what he says."

ʿĀ'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "I saw him receiving the revelation on a very cold day, and when it departed from him, there were beads of sweat on his forehead." Ibn Kathir notes that this was also reported in the Two Sahihs, and that the version quoted here is the one recorded by al-Bukhari.

Sit with that image. A cold day — and sweat on his blessed forehead. Whatever revelation was, it bore down on him. He himself said the harder of the two forms was the one that came with no visible messenger at all, only a sound like the ringing of a bell, from which he emerged having grasped exactly what was said.

And note the constant in both forms: *"I understand what was said."* However it came, it arrived understood.

## The One who reveals owns everything

"To Him belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is on the earth." Ibn Kathir's gloss is one line, and it covers everything: **everything is subject to His dominion and control.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the same connection the sūrah does — the One who has been sending prophets is such in His magnificence that whatever is in the heavens and in the earth is His; He is the Supreme, the Most Magnificent.

The ayah closes with **al-ʿAlī al-ʿAẓīm**, the Most High, the Most Great. Ibn Kathir points out that the Qur'an pairs these two ideas repeatedly — "the Most Great, the Most High" (13:9), "He is the Most High, the Most Great" (22:62) — and says there are many similar ayat. In the way of Ahl al-Sunnah, we affirm this loftiness and greatness as Allah has described Himself, without likening Him to any created thing and without emptying the words of their meaning.

## The heavens almost burst apart

"Nearly the heavens might be rent asunder from above them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān glosses the verb *yatafaṭṭarna* as **burst apart** — a splitting open, not a gentle strain. The heavens, the most immense structure we know, are described as on the verge of tearing.

Why? The sources give two explanations, and they are worth keeping side by side.

**First — out of fear of His might.** Ibn Kathir reports this from a striking list of early authorities: Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him), aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatādah, as-Suddī and Kaʿb al-Aḥbār. On this reading the near-bursting is awe.

**Second — under the sheer weight of the angels.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān follows this line. Even though some of the people of this world do not recognise and do not admit the greatness of His magnificence, the number of angels in the heavens who *do* know Him and recognise His greatness is so large that their load may quite likely cause the heavens to burst apart from above. A hadith narrated in Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah states that due to the large number of the angels, such crackling sounds are produced in the heavens as are produced when an excessive load is placed on something. And that is how it should be, the commentary continues, **because throughout the heavens there is not even a space of four fingers left vacant by angels who are in the state of prostration.**

On the physics of this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites *Bayān-ul-Qurʼān*: this tells us angels have weight, which is not beyond reason, because it is confirmed that angels also have physical bodies, even though very light in weight — and even light bodies add up to a considerable load when they are in huge numbers.

Try to picture the contrast the commentary itself draws. Below: people of this world who do not recognise or admit Allah's greatness. Above: angels so numerous that four fingers' width of empty sky cannot be found, packed in prostration, and the heavens groaning under them like an overloaded beam.

### The angels' two occupations

"…and the angels glorify the praises of their Lord, and ask for forgiveness for those on the earth."

Their first work, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it: they proclaim the perfection of their Lord and utter His praises. Their second work is to ask forgiveness — and its object is astonishing: **those on the earth**. Ibn Kathir sets this beside the ayah about the bearers of the Throne, who "ask forgiveness for those who believe, (saying): 'Our Lord! You comprehend all things in mercy and knowledge'" (40:7).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful here, and the care matters. The angels ask forgiveness even for the dwellers of this earth who do not give what is due to Allah's greatness, who instead indulge in associating others with Him and in infidelity, and who thereby become liable to suffer scourge. But that supplication is precisely bounded:

- it is **for a limited period only**, and limited to this world;
- it is a supplication that some severe worldly scourge may not befall the humans and destroy all of them;
- safety against the ordinary punishments of this world, and against the real scourge of the Hereafter, is **not** included in it.

And Allah, the Almighty, accepts this supplication and saves them from the general scourge in this world. So the calm a heedless person lives in may well be the answered prayer of angels he does not acknowledge — and it is bounded, not an acquittal.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a line that must not be blurred: it must be understood thoroughly that **Allah, and Allah alone, is the Forgiver and the Merciful** — the angels ask; He alone grants.

### "Lo! Verily, Allah is the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful"

Ibn Kathir's comment on this closing phrase is short: it is **a reminder, to take heed of this fact.**

Read it in sequence and it lands with force. The heavens are on the point of bursting; angels beyond counting are pressed into prostration; and the note the ayah closes on is not wrath but **al-Ghafūr ar-Raḥīm**. The same passage that makes you feel how small you are tells you where to run.

## Those who take protectors besides Him

"And as for those who take as protecting friends others besides Him — Allah is Ḥafīẓ over them, and you are not a trustee over them."

Ibn Kathir identifies who is meant: **the idolators**. And having just been told that all that is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, the reader can see what such a choice amounts to: seeking protection from what is itself under His dominion and control.

**Allāhu Ḥafīẓun ʿalayhim** — Ibn Kathir explains: He is **Witness to their deeds, recording and enumerating them precisely, and He will requite them for them in full.** Nothing is missed, nothing is approximated. The word is a warning to them; but read from the other side it is also why no wrong done to a believer is ever lost.

**"And you are not a trustee over them."** Ibn Kathir: *you are just a warner, and Allah is the Trustee of all affairs.*

This is where the passage turns tender. The Prophet ﷺ — the one who sweated in the cold under the weight of revelation — is told directly that their guidance is not his burden to carry. His task is to warn. Their record is already being kept by One who misses nothing, and the affairs belong to Allah.

## Living it

**Say the letters and let them humble you.** The sūrah opens with what only Allah knows. Approach the Qur'an as a receiver, not an auditor.

**Let the hadith of the sweat on a cold day change how you open the muṣḥaf.** These words came to him with weight. They deserve more than a distracted glance.

**Measure your own worship against the ceiling.** Not four fingers of empty sky, the commentary says — every space filled with prostration. Your unhurried sujūd joins something enormous already underway.

**Take the reprieve as a summons.** If safety from a general, sweeping scourge is in part the fruit of angels asking forgiveness for the people of the earth — and that request is bounded to this world only, covering neither ordinary worldly punishment nor the Hereafter — then the sane response is to use the time. *Alā inna Allāha huwa al-Ghafūru r-Raḥīm.*

**Check what you have taken as a protector besides Him.** Whatever you run to first when you are frightened, and whatever you believe is really keeping you safe — that is the question this last ayah is asking. Everything besides Allah that you might lean on is itself subject to His dominion and control.

**And put down what is not yours to carry.** Warn, advise, convey sincerely — then leave the outcome with Allah. He is the Trustee of all affairs; you were never appointed one.

passages.title: An Arabic Qur'an to warn the Mother of Cities
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat move from the revelation itself, to the Day it warns about, to the One who alone can protect you on that Day. Allah tells His Messenger ﷺ why this Qur'an came down in Arabic — to warn Makkah and everyone beyond it of the Day of Assembling, when humanity will be split into exactly two parties. Ayah 8 answers the question that division raises: could Allah not have made everyone one? And ayah 9 turns on the word that ayah 8 ends with — *walī*, protector — to expose the emptiness of every protector people take besides Him.

## The thread that ties the three together

Read the closing of ayah 8 and the opening of ayah 9 side by side and the seam becomes visible. Ayah 8 ends: "And the wrongdoers will have neither a protector (*walī*) nor a helper (*naṣīr*)." Ayah 9 immediately asks: "Or have they taken protecting friends (*awliyā'*) besides Him? But Allah — He Alone is the protector (*al-walī*)." The same word for protector returns three times in two breaths, once in the plural. The wrongdoer is told he has no *walī*; then we are shown him busily collecting *awliyā'*; then we are told where the only real one is. The passage is not a set of separate announcements. It is one argument: a warning is coming, a sorting is coming, and the only shelter is the One you were told to worship in the first place.

## "And thus We have revealed to you a Qur'an in Arabic" (ayah 7)

Ibn Kathir reads the opening — "and thus" — as Allah saying: *just as We sent revelation to the Prophets before you*, so We have revealed this to you. The Prophet ﷺ is not an innovation in history. He ﷺ stands in a line, receiving what those before him received.

On the phrase "a Qur'an in Arabic", Ibn Kathir's gloss is compact and worth sitting with: it means **plain, clear, and manifest**. The point is intelligibility. A warning that cannot be understood is not a warning. Allah sent the message in a form whose meanings are open and unhidden, so that no one at the receiving end could say the summons was obscure. Notice how this sets up the whole passage: the warning is *clear*, the Day is *without doubt*, the division is *only two*. Nothing here is left vague, because the stakes do not allow vagueness.

## Umm al-Qurā — the Mother of the Towns

"So that you may warn *Umm al-Qurā*." Ibn Kathir states plainly what the phrase names: **Makkah**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the image out: *Umm al-Qurā* means, in its words, "the origin and foundation of all habitations and cities," which is Makkah. A mother is where the rest comes from. Every other settlement is, in this framing, downstream of this one place.

Why does Makkah hold that rank? Both commentaries give the same answer: because in the sight of Allah it is nobler and more excellent than all other lands, cities and habitations. Ibn Kathir says this is established by much evidence discussed elsewhere, and then offers what he calls among the most concise and clear proofs of it — a report recorded by **Imam Ahmad** from 'Abdullah bin 'Adi bin Al-Hamra' Az-Zuhri, who heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say, as he ﷺ was standing in the market place of Makkah:

> "By Allah, you are the best land of Allah, the most beloved land to Allah; were it not for the fact that I was driven out from you, I would never have left you."

Ibn Kathir notes it was also recorded by **At-Tirmidhi, An-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah**, and that At-Tirmidhi said, "Hasan Sahih." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the same report from Imam Ahmad's *Musnad*, with the same grading from At-Tirmidhi, and adds the setting: he ﷺ spoke these words as he ﷺ was **migrating from the city**.

Sit with that scene, because it is the emotional centre of the passage. The Prophet ﷺ is being forced out of his home. He ﷺ stops in the market place — the ordinary, everyday trading heart of the town that has rejected him — and instead of cursing it, he ﷺ swears by Allah that it is the best land of Allah and the most beloved land to Allah, and says that nothing but expulsion could have made him leave. The ayah commissions him ﷺ to *warn* this city. The hadith shows us the heart with which he ﷺ carried out that commission. He ﷺ warned the people he loved most, in the place he loved most, and they drove him ﷺ out, and he ﷺ still loved it. That is what prophetic warning looks like from the inside: not the satisfaction of announcing someone's ruin, but the grief of a man who cannot bear the thought of them being ruined.

**"And all around it."** Ibn Kathir: this means "all the lands, east and west." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the widening circles — the suburbs in the neighbourhood of Makkah Mukarramah, then the neighbouring Arab countries, and then the whole of the earth from east to west. Makkah is the centre of the circle; the circumference is the world. Anyone reading this centuries away is inside "and all around it."

## The Day of Assembling, of which there is no doubt

"And warn them of the Day of Assembling" — *yawm al-jamʿ*. Ibn Kathir: this is the Day of Resurrection, "when Allah will assemble the first and the last in one plain." Everyone who has ever lived, from the first to the last, standing on a single plain. The name of the Day is taken from that single fact.

"Of which there is no doubt" — *lā rayba fīh*. Ibn Kathir's gloss is deliberately flat: there is no doubt that it will happen and will most certainly come to pass. The Qur'an does not argue the point here; it states it, and moves on to what it means for you.

Ibn Kathir places two other ayat alongside it to fill in the picture. First, "the Day when He will gather you all on the Day of Gathering — that will be the Day of mutual loss and gain" (64:9), which, he explains, means that the people of Paradise and the people of Hell will gain and lose respectively. Second, from Sūrat Hūd: "That is a Day whereon will be gathered together, and that is a Day when all will be present. And We delay it only for a term fixed. On the Day when it comes, no person shall speak except by His leave. Some among them will be wretched and others blessed" (11:103–105). Two details there sharpen the warning in our passage: the delay is not indefinite, it is a fixed term; and on that Day nobody speaks except by His leave. The mouths that argue loudest here will be silent there.

## "A party in Paradise and a party in the blazing Fire"

The ayah ends the sentence with a split — *farīq*, rendered "a party" — and offers no third option. There is no middle destination named, and no unassigned remainder.

On this phrase Ibn Kathir brings a striking report recorded by **Imam Ahmad** from 'Abdullah bin 'Amr (may Allah be pleased with him). The Messenger of Allah ﷺ came out to them holding two books in his hand and asked, "Do you know what these two books are?" They said, "We do not know unless you tell us, O Messenger of Allah." Concerning the book in his right hand, he ﷺ said: "This is a book from the Lord of the worlds, containing the names of the people of Paradise and of their fathers and tribes; all of them are detailed, down to the last one of them, and nothing will be added or taken away from it." Concerning the book in his left hand, he ﷺ said the same of the people of Hell.

The Companions asked the honest question — the one any believer feels: "Why should we strive if it is something that is already cut and dried?" His answer ﷺ:

> "Strive with your deeds as hard as you can for middle course or close to it, for the person who is destined for Paradise will die doing the deeds of the people of Paradise, regardless of what he did before, and the person who is destined for Hell will die doing the deeds of the people of Hell, regardless of what he did before."

Then he ﷺ made a gesture with his fist and said, "Your Lord has settled the matter of His servants," and he ﷺ opened his right hand as if throwing something — "a party in Paradise" — and made a similar gesture with his left hand — "and a party in the blazing Fire." Ibn Kathir notes this was also recorded by **At-Tirmidhi and An-Nasa'i**, and that At-Tirmidhi said, "Hasan Sahih Gharib."

Notice what the answer does *not* do. It does not unravel the mystery of the decree; it redirects you away from a question you cannot answer toward the one thing you can act on. You have no access to the books. You have access to your next deed. And the sign given is the **ending** — what a person is doing when death finds him — which is precisely what keeps both fear and hope alive to the last breath.

Ibn Kathir follows this with another report from Imam Ahmad, from Abu Nadrah, about a Companion of the Prophet ﷺ named Abu Abdullah, whom his friends found weeping. They asked what had caused him to weep, reminding him that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had said to him, "Trim your moustache and adhere to that practice until you meet me." He said yes — but he had also heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say that Allah, may He be exalted, picked up a handful in His Right Hand and another in His other Hand, and said, "This is for this and this is for this, and I do not care." And the man said: "**And I do not know in which of the two handfuls I am.**" Ibn Kathir adds that there are several hadiths about *al-Qadr*, the Divine Decree, in the books of Sahih, Sunan and Musnad, including those narrated by 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, 'A'ishah and a large number of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all.

The practical lesson is in the tears of that Companion. A man who had been addressed personally by the Prophet ﷺ, and told to hold to a practice "until you meet me," still wept — because what he had heard about himself did not include the one thing he wanted to know. That is the posture the report leaves us in: full hope in Allah, and no confidence at all in one's own guarantees.

## "And if Allah had willed, He could have made them one nation" (ayah 8)

Here the Qur'an anticipates the objection. If the split into two parties is so grave, why is humanity split at all? Ibn Kathir answers: had Allah willed, He could have made them one single nation — "either all following guidance or all following misguidance." Uniformity was fully within His power. He made them all different instead. He guides whomsoever He wills to the truth and sends astray whomsoever He wills, and — Ibn Kathir is careful to add both halves — "He has complete wisdom and perfect proof."

Those two phrases carry the weight of the whole matter. **Complete wisdom**: the arrangement is not arbitrary, even where we cannot trace the reason. **Perfect proof**: no one whom the warning reached can claim they were not told. That is exactly why ayah 7 stressed a Qur'an that is "plain, clear, and manifest," delivered to the Mother of the Towns and to all around it. The argument has been laid out in the open. Nobody is condemned on a technicality.

Then the mercy: "**but He admits whom He wills to His mercy.**" Look at the asymmetry in the sentence. Entry into mercy is stated as something Allah actively does — He admits people into it. The other side is stated as a bare absence: "and the wrongdoers will have neither a protector nor a helper." Mercy is described by what Allah gives; loss is described by what the wrongdoer simply does not have. They are left standing exactly where they insisted on standing, without the two things every human being in trouble reaches for — someone with the standing to shelter them (*walī*) and someone with the strength to rescue them (*naṣīr*).

## "Or have they taken protecting friends besides Him?" (ayah 9)

And so we arrive at the question. Ibn Kathir reads this as Allah **denouncing the idolaters for taking other gods instead of Allah**, declaring that He is the True Deity, and that it is not right to worship anyone except Him Alone.

The form matters. The ayah does not first argue that the false objects of worship are powerless; it asks the question and then answers it with a sentence that leaves no room: "**But Allah — He Alone is the protector.**" Not one protector among several. The only one there is.

Then comes the proof, and it is precisely the credential the situation demands: "**And He Who gives life to the dead, and He is Able to do all things.**" Ibn Kathir: He is the One Who is able to bring the dead back to life, and He is Able to do all things. Read that against ayah 7 and the passage closes its own circle. You were warned about the Day when the first and the last are assembled in one plain. Who could possibly be your *walī* on such a Day? Only the One who gives life to the dead in the first place. Every other patron you might cultivate will himself be standing on that plain, unable to speak except by His leave. A protector who is himself being judged cannot protect you from the Judge.

## Living it

**Take the clarity seriously.** The Qur'an was revealed "plain, clear, and manifest." That is a mercy and a responsibility: the reason it was made clear was so that it would be understood. Reading it for meaning, not only for sound, is what the ayah is asking of you.

**Warn the way he ﷺ warned.** He ﷺ stood in the market place of the city that expelled him and told it that it was the best land of Allah and the most beloved land to Allah. Whatever warning you carry to others, carry it with that love, not against them.

**Answer the question about the decree the way he ﷺ answered it.** Not with speculation, but with: *strive with your deeds as hard as you can, aim for the middle course or close to it, and keep going.* The books are written and none of us has read them. What we have is the next action.

**Audit your protectors.** Ayah 9's question is not addressed only to people bowing before idols. It exposes anyone who has quietly relocated their sense of safety — into wealth, into status, into a person, into their own competence. Ask honestly what you lean on when you are frightened. Then put it back where it belongs: "But Allah — He Alone is the protector. And He Who gives life to the dead, and He is Able to do all things."

passages.title: Allah alone judges, originates, and provides
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat answer one question from three directions: **who is actually in charge?** Allah alone settles what people differ over (ayah 10), alone originates the heavens and the earth and keeps creating generation after generation (ayah 11), and alone holds the keys, expanding and restricting provision (ayah 12). Law, life, livelihood — three things human beings most want to control, and none of them is ours.

## The argument they belong to

Ibn Kathir does not treat these ayat as a fresh start. He reads them together with ayah 9: *"Or have they taken protecting friends besides Him? But Allah — He Alone is the protector. And He Who gives life to the dead, and He is Able to do all things."* He heads the whole section **"Allah is the Protector, Ruler and Creator"**, and explains that here Allah denounces the idolaters for taking other gods instead of Allah, declaring that He is the True Deity, that it is not right to worship anyone except Him alone, and that He is the One able to bring the dead back to life and Able to do all things.

That sets the frame. The question on the table is about protection and patronage — who you belong to, and who you turn to. Ayat 10–12 answer it by naming three areas where every human being needs a patron.

## Ayah 10: "Whatever you differ in, its judgment lies with Allah"

The Arabic is deliberately wide open: *wa mā ikhtalaftum fīhi min shay'* — "and whatever thing you have differed over." Ibn Kathir's comment is short and sweeping: it means "in whatever issue you differ. **This is general in meaning and applies to all things.**" No category of dispute is carved out.

But notice how carefully he then explains *how* Allah judges. *Fa-ḥukmuhu ilā Allāh* — "the decision thereof is with Allah" — "means, He is the Judge of that, **according to His Book and the Sunnah of His Prophet ﷺ**." Allah has already spoken; referring a dispute to Him means referring it to what He revealed. Ibn Kathir supports this by placing beside it the instruction of Sūrah an-Nisā': *"(And) if you differ in anything amongst yourselves, refer it to Allah and His Messenger"* (4:59).

The translation in front of us frames the ayah as something the Prophet ﷺ is told to *say* to the believers. So this is not only a statement about Allah; it is a posture the Messenger ﷺ is taught to voice for his community.

### Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: if judgment is Allah's, what about obeying people?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes up exactly the objection an alert reader raises. The judgment in all disputed matters lies with Allah, it says, **because sovereignty belongs to Allah only** — and it cites another ayah as proof: *"The Decision belongs to none but Allah"* (6:57).

Then the difficulty: the Qur'an in many places directs us to obey Rasulullah ﷺ, and in some places to obey those in authority. Does that not contradict what was just declared?

Maʿārif answers that there is no contradiction, because the orders of Rasulullah ﷺ and of those in authority are also, *in a way*, orders of Allah. It lays out the basis:

- **Direct revelation.** If the order has been received through *waḥy* (revelation), or is based upon the clear and definite verses — the *nuṣūṣ* — of the Qur'an and Sunnah, then its being an order of Allah is obvious.
- **Reasoned inference.** If the order is an *ijtihād* (an inference) which in turn is based upon the *nuṣūṣ* of Qur'an and Sunnah, then also, in a way, it is an order of Allah. On this basis, Maʿārif says, the *ijtihādāt* of the *mujtahidīn* of the ummah — those competent to interpret the Qur'an and Sunnah and infer Islamic laws from them — are included in the orders of Allah.
- **The ordinary believer's access.** That is why, it concludes, the learned scholars have declared that the *fatwā* (ruling) given by a *muftī* (a competent Islamic scholar) is to be taken as part of the religious law by the common masses, who do not have the ability to understand the Qur'an and the Sunnah directly.

The logic is worth sitting with. "Judgment belongs to Allah" is not a slogan against scholarship or against legitimate authority. Maʿārif's entire argument turns on a chain: the ruling counts as an order of Allah *because* it rests on the clear texts of Qur'an and Sunnah, whether directly or through qualified inference. That basis is the whole of the reasoning.

### "Such is Allah, my Lord"

*Dhālikumu-llāhu Rabbī.* Ibn Kathir glosses this simply: it means "(He is) the Judge of all things." The demonstrative *dhālikum* — "**that** is Allah" — gathers up everything just said and points at it: the One who gives life to the dead, who alone protects, who alone decides — *that* One is my Lord.

Then the ayah turns personal in a way that is easy to rush past. Having stated the truth about Allah, the Prophet ﷺ is taught to state his own response to it:

**ʿalayhi tawakkaltu wa ilayhi unīb** — "in Whom I put my trust, and to Him I turn in repentance."

Ibn Kathir renders the meaning of both clauses in one phrase: *"I refer all matters to Him."* Two motions sit in the words themselves. *Tawakkul* is putting your trust in Allah — depending on Him. *Ināba* is turning to Him, in repentance. Forward and back, both aimed at the same point: referring everything to Him.

And the placement is the lesson. The natural human response to "the decision belongs to Allah" is anxiety — *then I am not in control.* The ayah models a different response: if the decision is His, then trust Him and turn to Him. What you believe about Allah is not left as information; it is immediately converted into where the heart rests.

## Ayah 11: the Originator, and the pairs

*Fāṭir as-samāwāti wa'l-arḍ* — "the Originator of the heavens and the earth." Ibn Kathir explains this as "the Maker of them both **and everything in between**." Not only the two great structures but everything held inside them.

Then the ayah narrows sharply from the heavens to your own household:

- **"He has made for you mates from yourselves"** — Ibn Kathir: "of your own kind. **As a blessing and a favour from Him**, He has made your kind male and female." Note that he reads this as a kindness, not merely a mechanism. That your spouse is of your own kind is itself named as a favour.
- **"and for the cattle also mates"** — Ibn Kathir: "He has created for you eight pairs of cattle."
- **"By this means He creates you"** (*yadhra'ukum fīhi*) — Ibn Kathir: "in this manner He creates you, male and female, **generation after generation** of men and cattle."

That last phrase is the point of the sequence. Creation in this ayah is not only a finished event in the distant past. Allah made your kind male and female, and in this manner He creates you — generation after generation, human and cattle alike.

### "There is nothing like Him"

*Laysa ka-mithlihi shay'.* And now watch where Ibn Kathir places the emphasis: "there is nothing like **the Creator of these pairs**, for He is the Unique, the Self-Sufficient Master, Who has no peer or equal."

The negation lands exactly where the ayah has been building. The ayah has just been naming things that come in matched pairs — your own kind made male and female, the eight pairs of cattle. And the Creator of those pairs, Ibn Kathir says, has no peer and no equal. Nothing is like Him.

And in the very same ayah, immediately after likeness is denied, two names are affirmed: *wa huwa as-Samīʿ al-Baṣīr* — "and He is the All-Hearer, the All-Seer." The ayah itself sets these side by side. The One who has no equal is not remote from you: He is the All-Hearer and the All-Seer.

## Ayah 12: the keys

*Lahu maqālīd as-samāwāti wa'l-arḍ* — "To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth"; the translation adds "the keys **of the treasuries**." Ibn Kathir notes that he has already discussed the interpretation of this phrase in Sūrat az-Zumar (39:63), and gives the conclusion: **He is the One Who is controlling and governing them.**

So the image of keys is not a title on paper. Ibn Kathir reads it as live control and governance of the heavens and the earth.

Which is why the ayah moves straight from keys to provision: **"He expands provision for whom He wills, and straitens."** Ibn Kathir: "He gives plentiful provision to whomsoever He wills and He reduces it for whomsoever He wills, **and He is perfectly Wise and Just.**"

Do not skip that closing clause. The ayah could have left us with bare will — He gives to some, withholds from others. Ibn Kathir's words are the comfort of the verse: the One who expands and restricts is perfectly Wise and Just. And the ayah seals it: *"Verily, He is the All-Knower of everything."* He is not apportioning in ignorance of your situation.

## The names that close each ayah

Read the three endings together and you see the passage tightening:

- Ayah 10 — **my Lord**, the Judge of all things, in whom I put my trust and to whom I turn.
- Ayah 11 — **the All-Hearer, the All-Seer**, the One with nothing like Him.
- Ayah 12 — **the All-Knower of everything**, to whom the keys belong.

Judgment belongs to the One who is the All-Hearer, the All-Seer, the All-Knower of everything. That is why referring matters to Him is not resignation.

## Living it

**When you differ, know where the case goes.** Ibn Kathir's reading is general: it "applies to all things." And his method is specific: the decision is Allah's *according to His Book and the Sunnah of His Prophet ﷺ*. So a disagreement — in a marriage, in business, in the community, in your own head — is referred to what Allah revealed, as 4:59 instructs. And where you cannot read the sources yourself, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's guidance applies plainly: the fatwā of a competent scholar is to be taken as part of the religious law by those who cannot understand the Qur'an and Sunnah directly.

**Convert the belief immediately.** The Prophet ﷺ is taught to follow the statement with *"in Him I put my trust, and to Him I turn in repentance."* Make the same move: refer all matters to Him, as Ibn Kathir puts it.

**See your family as the ayah sees it.** A spouse of your own kind is named here as a blessing and a favour from Him, and each arriving generation is named as Him creating. That reframes ordinary domestic life as a place where His act is visible.

**Hold provision loosely.** He holds the keys; He gives plentifully to whom He wills and reduces for whom He wills; and He is perfectly Wise and Just, the All-Knower of everything. Neither abundance nor tightness is outside that.

**Let *"there is nothing like Him"* discipline your imagination.** He is the Unique, the Self-Sufficient Master, who has no peer or equal — so no comparison drawn from what you have seen will reach Him. And in the same breath the ayah tells you He is the All-Hearer, the All-Seer: near enough to hear you now, and to see you now.

passages.title: One religion of all prophets, split by envy
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat make one argument: the religion given to this Ummah is not a new invention but the same religion Allah entrusted to Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa and 'Isa — so the duty is to *establish* it and refuse to splinter over it.

## "He has ordained for you" — the same religion, five names

Ma'ariful Qur'an notes the placement: the earlier ayat spoke of Allah's visible, material blessings; from here the subject is the inner, spiritual blessing — that He has given you the very religion common to all the Prophets.

Ibn Kathir points out the shape of the list: Allah names **the first Messenger sent after Adam — Nuh** — and **the last of them, Muhammad ﷺ** ("that which We have revealed to you"), and between them those whom Ibn Kathir calls **the Messengers of strong will: Ibrahim, Musa and 'Isa son of Maryam**. The same five appear together in Surat al-Ahzab, where Allah takes the covenant of the Prophets: "and from you, and from Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, and 'Isa son of Maryam" (33:7).

Ma'ariful Qur'an adds a reason for the order here. Nuh comes first; Ibrahim sits in the middle because he is the father of prophets and was acknowledged as a prophet even by the Arabs despite their disbelief and shirk; Musa and 'Isa follow because it was *their* followers who were present while the Qur'an was being revealed. And there is a difference between the two lists: in Surat al-Ahzab the Prophet ﷺ is mentioned **before** Nuh, while here Nuh is mentioned before him. Ma'ariful Qur'an suggests this may indicate that although Muhammad ﷺ was born and sent as a prophet after all the others, he preceded everyone else in the originally destined (*azali*) distribution of prophethood and messengership. It cites the hadith, "I preceded all the other prophets in the original creation and I am last of all the prophets in being sent" — reported by Ibn Majah and Darimi from Bahz ibn Hakim, rated *hasan* (see Mishkah).

**Why does the list not begin with Adam?** Ma'ariful Qur'an answers: Adam shares fully in the principles of belief, but in his time disbelief and shirk had not yet appeared among people. Confrontation with kufr and shirk begins with Nuh, so the sequence starts with him. (And Allah knows best.)

## What "one religion" does and does not mean

The unity is at the root, not in every branch. Ibn Kathir states the common message plainly: every Messenger came to call to the worship of Allah alone, with no partner — "And We did not send any Messenger before you but We revealed to him: None has the right to be worshipped but I, so worship Me" (21:25). A hadith of the Prophet ﷺ is quoted here: **"We Prophets are brothers and our religion is one."** (Ibn Kathir relays this saying without naming a collection.) The bond, Ibn Kathir explains, is that Allah alone is worshipped, with no partner — "even though their laws and ways may differ," as Allah says: "To each among you, We have prescribed a law and a clear way" (5:48).

So there are two layers. Ma'ariful Qur'an spells out the first: the *din* common to all the Prophets is belief in the Oneness of Allah, in prophethood, in the life after death; the principles of worship such as salah, fasting, hajj and zakah; and the prohibitions of theft, robbery, adultery, telling lies, deceit, hurting others without a valid reason, and breach of promise. These have been the common injunctions of every divine religion. The second layer is the detail of the revealed law, which 5:48 shows differs from prophet to prophet. Ma'ariful Qur'an concludes that the order to establish the religion and the prohibition of dissension pertain to those divine laws that have been common and consistent across the codes of all the prophets.

## "Establish the religion, and be not divided in it"

The particle *an* before this command means the ayah is now unpacking what "He has ordained" consisted of.

- **Establish it.** Qurtubi, as cited by Ma'ariful Qur'an, glosses "establishing the din" as holding on to the rules of religion steadfastly, not letting any doubt or distrust creep into it, and not giving it up in any case.
- **Do not divide over it.** Ibn Kathir reads this as an injunction laid on all the Prophets, peace be upon them: Allah enjoined them to be as one and forbade them to differ and be divided.

Ma'ariful Qur'an gathers the Sunnah on this. **Ibn Mas'ud** relates that one day the Messenger of Allah ﷺ drew a straight line in front of them, then drew other small lines to its right and left, and said that the lines on the right and left were the ways invented by devils, each of those ways controlled by a Shaitan who incites people to follow it; then, pointing to the straight line, he recited, "And this is My path, straight. So follow it" (6:153). (Ahmad, an-Nasa'i, Darimi — via Mazhari.) The straight path here is the religion common to all the Prophets.

Two more narrations are cited: the Prophet ﷺ said that the person who moves away even one span from the general body of Muslims has taken the neck-band of Islam off his neck (Ahmad, Abu Dawud); and **Ibn 'Abbas** stated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Allah's hand is upon the general body" (Tirmidhi, rated *hasan*). And **Mu'adh ibn Jabal** narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said that for humans, Shaitan is like a wolf after a herd of goats, catching hold of the goat that has strayed away from the herd — "so stay with the general body, and do not separate yourself." (Ahmad, as quoted by Tafsir Mazhari.)

**An essential qualification.** Ma'ariful Qur'an is careful to say that differences of opinion between the leading *mujtahidin* — qualified scholars exercising reasoned judgement — in ancillary matters, where the Qur'an and hadith carry no express ruling, or where the texts appear to pull in different directions and opinions are bound to differ, bear no relation to the dissension forbidden here. Such differences have continued since the days of the Prophet ﷺ, beginning with the noble Companions themselves, and the jurists unanimously consider them a blessing. What is forbidden is manufacturing division in what is unanimously agreed.

## Too heavy for them to carry

"Intolerable for the idolators is that to which you call them." Ibn Kathir: it is too much for them to bear, and they hate what you call them to, O Muhammad — that is, *tawhid* itself. Ma'ariful Qur'an adds the diagnosis: the call to Allah's Oneness seems very difficult to the polytheists even though it has been proved true by the consensus of all the prophets — because they follow their desires and the teachings of Shaitan, and have therefore strayed from the right path.

## Two ways to the straight path (end of ayah 13)

"Allah chooses for Himself whom He wills, and guides unto Himself who turns to Him." Ma'ariful Qur'an draws out two distinct ways a person comes to the straight path:

1. **Allah selects him.** Allah Himself picks a person out for the straight path of His religion and moulds his nature and inclinations accordingly — as happens with the prophets and His special friends. Of such He says, "We chose them for a trait: the remembrance of the [eternal] Home" (38:46), and the Qur'an uses the word *mukhlasin*, "chosen ones", for certain prophets. This way of guidance is exceptional and limited.
2. **He turns towards Allah.** The general route, open to everyone: when someone turns towards Allah and intends to follow His din, Allah guides him to it.

Ibn Kathir summarises the clause as: He is the One who decrees guidance for those who deserve it and decrees misguidance for those who prefer it to the right path. And Ma'ariful Qur'an closes the loop on the Makkans: the reason the call to Oneness was so hard on them is that they did not even have the intention of understanding and following the truth.

## Ayah 14: they split *after* the knowledge came

Division was not caused by ignorance or genuine confusion. Ibn Kathir: their opposition to the truth arose *after* it had come to them and proof had been established against them; nothing made them resist in that way except their transgression and stubbornness. The ayah itself frames the split as happening "in jealousy with each other".

**Who is "they"?** Ma'ariful Qur'an records two readings. **Ibn 'Abbas** held that the pronoun refers to the Quraysh of Makkah: their aversion to the straight path would have been utter ignorance in itself, but on top of that they persisted after knowledge had been imparted by Allah — and by that imparting of knowledge Ibn 'Abbas means the coming of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who was the source of all divine knowledge. Some scholars, however, refer the pronoun to past communities: the people of bygone ummahs created dissension in the true faith of their respective prophets and adopted separate ways, despite having received the knowledge of the straight path from those prophets. Either way, Ma'ariful Qur'an notes, the pagans of Makkah and the disbelievers of earlier ages alike demanded that their prophets follow the misguidance they themselves had adopted — and that is exactly what ayah 15 answers.

**"Had it not been for a Word that went forth from your Lord for an appointed term."** Ibn Kathir: were it not that Allah had already decreed to delay the reckoning of His servants until the Day of Resurrection, the punishment would have been hastened for them in this world. The delay you are living in is a decree, not an oversight.

**"Those who were made to inherit the Scripture after them are in grave doubt concerning it."** Ibn Kathir explains this as the later generation that came after the earlier generation which had rejected the truth: they have no firm conviction in matters of religion. They merely imitate their forefathers, without any evidence or proof, and so they are very confused and doubtful — inherited religion without knowledge settles no heart.

## Ayah 15: ten commands in a single verse

Ibn Kathir notes something remarkable here, and Ma'ariful Qur'an repeats it: this ayah includes **ten separate and independent ideas, each of which is a ruling in its own right**, and the scholars said there is nothing else like it in the Qur'an except Ayat al-Kursi (2:255), which likewise includes ten.

1. **"So unto this then invite."** Ibn Kathir: call people to this which We have revealed to you and enjoined upon all the Prophets before you. Ma'ariful Qur'an: although your call to *tawhid* sits very heavily on the polytheists, that is no reason to give it up.
2. **"And stand firm as you are commanded."** Ibn Kathir: adhere firmly — you and those who follow you — to the worship of Allah as He has commanded you. Ma'ariful Qur'an: this firmness must be in accordance with the command of Allah, meaning moderate in beliefs, deeds, morals, habits and social behaviour, with not the slightest inclination towards *ifrat* (overdoing something) or *tafrit* (falling short in something). Obviously such firmness is not easy — which is why, when some noble Companions pointed out that some of his hairs had turned grey, the Prophet ﷺ said, **"Surah Hud has turned me old"**; the same command is given in Surah Hud in these very words.
3. **"And follow not their desires."** Ibn Kathir: the desires of the idolaters, in the falsehoods they invented and fabricated by worshipping idols. Ma'ariful Qur'an: he is directed not to be concerned about the opposition of any opponent in his duty of conveying the message.
4. **"Say: I believe in whatever Book Allah has sent down."** Ibn Kathir: I believe in all the Books revealed from heaven to the Prophets; we do not differentiate between any of them. Ma'ariful Qur'an: he believes not only in the Book revealed to him but in all the former divine books.
5. **"And I am commanded to do justice among you."** Ibn Kathir: when judging according to the commands of Allah. Ma'ariful Qur'an notes some exegetes take *'adl* here as "equality" — treating all the commands of religion equally, by believing in every prophet and every Book and obeying all the divine laws without exception.
6. **"Allah is our Lord and your Lord."** Ibn Kathir: He is the One who is to be worshipped, and there is no true god but He. We affirm this willingly, and even though you do not do so willingly, everyone in the universe prostrates to Him obediently. Ma'ariful Qur'an: all of us are nourished by Allah.
7. **"For us our deeds and for you your deeds."** Ibn Kathir: we have nothing to do with you — like 10:41, "You are innocent of what I do, and I am innocent of what you do." Ma'ariful Qur'an: our deeds are for us only and you neither gain nor lose by them, and your deeds are for you only.
8. **"There is no dispute between us and you."** Mujahid: this means, no argument. Ma'ariful Qur'an: since the disbelievers do not accept the truth despite its having been proved, which demonstrates their enmity, further discussion is useless.
9. **"Allah will assemble us."** Ibn Kathir: on the Day of Resurrection — as in 34:26, "Our Lord will assemble us all together, then He will judge between us with truth." Ma'ariful Qur'an: He will gather all of us and requite every deed.
10. **"And to Him is the final return."** Ibn Kathir: the final return on the Day of Reckoning.

**Was any of this abrogated?** As-Suddi said this was before the Ayah of the sword was revealed, and Ibn Kathir considers that to fit the context, since this ayah was revealed in Makkah while the Ayah of the sword (22:39–40) was revealed after the Hijrah. Ma'ariful Qur'an reports both positions: some exegetes hold that the verses conveying the command for jihad cancelled this command, because the essence of jihad is to subjugate by fighting those who do not accept advice and exhortation — not to leave them in the state of kufr; and some exegetes hold that this command has not been cancelled at all, its meaning being that since the truth has been proved through logical arguments, its non-acceptance can only be due to enmity and obstinacy, and so everybody is responsible for his own deeds (Qurtubi).

## Ayah 16: arguing after the call has been answered

Ibn Kathir: here Allah warns those who try to hinder those who believe in Allah from following His path. "Those who dispute concerning Allah **after it has been accepted**": Ma'ariful Qur'an glosses the phrase as *after many people responded to the call of His prophets by accepting Islam*.

**Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid** said: they disputed with the believers after those believers had responded to Allah and His Messenger, and tried to prevent them from following the path of guidance, hoping that they would return to Jahiliyyah. **Qatadah** said these were the Jews and Christians who told the Muslims, "Our religion is better than your religion, our Prophet came before your Prophet, and we are better than you and closer to Allah than you" — which, Ibn Kathir says, was nothing but lies. Ma'ariful Qur'an records both this and a second report: that the same argument was put forward by the disbelievers of Quraysh, because they called themselves followers of the religion of Ibrahim.

The verdict is threefold: **"their dispute is futile before their Lord"** (Ibn Kathir: it is futile before Allah), **"upon them is wrath"** — from Him — and **"for them is a severe torment"**, on the Day of Resurrection. Ma'ariful Qur'an sums up the warning: the explanations and proofs in favour of Islam and the Qur'an were fully provided to you, and your own sensible and fair-minded people, having accepted them, embraced Islam; what you are doing now is nothing but falsehood and misguidance, and if you do not accept it, divine punishment will visit you.

## Living it

- **Two duties, not one.** Establishing the din — Qurtubi's "hold on steadfastly, let no doubt creep in, do not give it up in any case" — and refusing to fracture over it come in the same breath.
- **Know the difference between division and scholarly difference.** Manufacturing splits in what is unanimously agreed is what is condemned; the reasoned differences of qualified scholars in ancillary matters are, by unanimous verdict of the jurists, a blessing.
- **Stay with the general body.** The wolf takes the goat that strays from the herd.
- **Diagnose your own resistance.** Ayah 14 indicts not the ignorant but those to whom knowledge had already come and who still resisted, out of jealousy and stubbornness. That is a mirror worth holding up.
- **Invite, stand firm, and do not be dragged.** The ten commands of ayah 15 are a whole posture: keep calling, stay moderate, refuse the opponents' desires, honour every earlier Book, be just, and leave the verdict to the Day when Allah assembles everyone.

passages.title: The Book, the Balance, and the near Hour
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat answer the arrogance of the previous ayah with three quiet, immense facts: Allah is the One who sent down revelation and justice, the Hour He has promised may be nearer than anyone imagines, and He is meanwhile gentle and generous with the very servants He will one day judge. What holds them together is a single movement — from **the standard** (the Book and the Balance), to **the reckoning** against that standard (the Hour), to **the One** who set the standard, fixed the reckoning, and still feeds every creature in the meantime.

## The argument being answered

Ibn Kathir reads ayah 17 as Allah's reply to the people described just before it, in ayah 16 — "those who dispute concerning Allah, after it has been accepted." These are people who argue with believers *after* those believers have already responded to Allah and His Messenger, trying to stop them from following the path of guidance. Ibn Kathir says their dispute is futile before Allah, that upon them is wrath from Him, and that a severe torment awaits them on the Day of Resurrection.

Who were they? Ibn Kathir preserves two explanations. **Ibn 'Abbas** (may Allah be pleased with him) and **Mujahid** said they argued with the believers after those believers had answered the call, hoping to pull them back into Jahiliyyah — back into the ignorance they had just walked out of. **Qatadah** said they were Jews and Christians who told the Muslims: "Our religion is better than your religion, our Prophet came before your Prophet, and we are better than you and closer to Allah than you." Ibn Kathir's verdict on that claim is blunt: it was nothing but lies.

So the tone of ayah 17 is set. Against loud claims of superiority, Allah does not argue about pedigree. He simply states who He is and what He has done.

## Ayah 17: the Book and the Balance

**"It is Allah Who has sent down the Book in truth, and the Balance."**

Notice first *which* Book. Ibn Kathir says this refers to **all the Books which were revealed from Him to His Prophets**, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same: "the Book" here means the Qur'an and all the previously revealed Books. That is precisely the point against Qatadah's disputants. They were boasting that their scripture came first. Allah answers that every scripture came from one Sender — so a Book cannot be a trophy to wave at someone else. Being *given* a Book was never the achievement; the achievement is what you do with it.

**The Balance.** The Arabic word is *mīzān*, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes literally means a weighing balance — the physical instrument tradesmen use. Since a balance exists to weigh out what someone is owed and so to establish fairness, **Ibn 'Abbas** understood *mīzān* here as equity and justice. **Mujahid** — whom Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls a leading exegete — said it means full payment of everyone's rights and doing justice. Ibn Kathir reports the same understanding, "justice and fairness," from both Mujahid and Qatadah.

Ibn Kathir then places this alongside two other passages that pair the same two words:

- "Indeed We have sent Our Messengers with clear proofs, and revealed with them the Scripture and the Balance that mankind may keep up justice" (57:25). Revelation was never meant to stay on a shelf; it came so that human beings would actually stand justice up among themselves.
- "And the heaven He has raised high, and He has set up the Balance. In order that you may not transgress (due) balance. And observe the weight with equity and do not make the balance deficient" (55:7-9). There the same word arcs from the order of the heavens down to the scale in a shopkeeper's hand.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the structure of the ayah beautifully. It takes "truth" (*al-ḥaqq*) here to mean the divine religion mentioned earlier in the sūrah — so **"the Book with the truth" points to Allah's rights over His servants, and "the Balance" points to the rights of human beings over one another.** In one short sentence Allah names both halves of religion. A man who guards his prayer and shortchanges his customers has taken the Book and dropped the Balance. A man scrupulous in his dealings who has no room for his Lord has taken the Balance and dropped the Book. Allah sent down both, together, from one hand.

## "And what can make you know — perhaps the Hour is near?"

The sentence turns without warning. Having named the standard, Allah names the moment the standard will be applied.

The phrasing is not a piece of information; it is a question left open. Ibn Kathir gives it three effects at once. It is **encouragement to strive** for the sake of the Hour; it is **a terrifying warning**; and it is **advice to think little of this world**. Read it again with those three in mind. Nobody is told *when*. Everyone is told that it could be soon — and uncertainty of that kind does something to a person that a date on a calendar never could. A known date can be procrastinated against. An unknown nearness cannot.

This also quietly settles the dispute of ayah 16. People arguing about whose religion is older are arguing about the past. Allah points them at what is coming.

## Ayah 18: two hearts, one Hour

The next ayah sorts humanity by how they *react* to that nearness — and the split is not between the informed and the ignorant, but between two kinds of heart.

**"Those who believe not therein seek to hasten it."** Ibn Kathir explains what their hurry actually is: they say, *when will this promise be fulfilled, if you are telling the truth?* But they say it out of disbelief and stubbornness, thinking the whole thing unlikely to happen. It is not a request for a date. It is a taunt. You only demand that a threat arrive early when you are certain it is empty.

**"While those who believe are fearful of it, and know that it is the very truth."** Ibn Kathir says simply: they are afraid of it happening — and they know it will undoubtedly come to pass, *so they prepare themselves for it and strive for its sake*. That last clause is the whole difference. The disbelievers' certainty produces mockery; the believers' certainty produces work.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān refines what this fear is made of. It is fear born of two kinds of awareness: awareness of the awesome, terrifying events that will take place on that Day, and awareness of one's own shortcomings and wrongdoing. So it is not a vague dread of the universe. It is a man who knows both what is coming and what he has been doing.

And then a merciful qualification, which many readers need: **sometimes a believer's eagerness to meet his Lord overcomes that fear, and this does not contradict the ayah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that some of the dead have been reported to say in their graves that they wish the Day would come soon — because the glad tidings brought to them by the angels, that they would be forgiven and treated kindly, had overcome their fear of it. So the ayah describes the believer's normal posture, not a rule that a believer may never long for his Lord. Fear and longing are both real, and in a healthy heart they take turns.

## From the Sunnah: "What have you prepared for it?"

Ibn Kathir cites a report he says came through various chains of narration, in numbers reaching the level of *mutawātir* — that is, so many independent chains that the report is beyond doubt — in authentic (*ṣaḥīḥ*) and good (*ḥasan*) narrations found in the books of *Sunan* and *Musnad*.

A man called out to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in a loud voice while he was on one of his journeys: "O Muhammad!" The Prophet ﷺ answered him in the same manner: "Here I am!" The man asked, "When will the Hour come?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> **"Woe to you! It will most certainly come. What have you done to prepare for it?"**

The man answered: "Love for Allah and His Messenger." The Prophet ﷺ said:

> **"You will be with those whom you love."**

And in another narration: **"A man will be with those whom he loves."** Ibn Kathir says this is *mutawātir* beyond a doubt.

Then he draws the lesson, and it is the exact lesson of ayah 17: **he ﷺ did not answer the question of *when* the Hour would happen — he commanded the man to prepare for it.** The Qur'an withheld the date and pressed the question; the Prophet ﷺ did the same. When we find ourselves fascinated by timing, this is the redirection.

There is something else worth pausing on. The man had no long record of deeds to offer — only love. And the answer he received was not a rebuke but one of the greatest promises in the religion. Loving Allah and His Messenger is itself preparation, because love pulls a life after it.

## "Those who dispute concerning the Hour are in far-gone error"

Ayah 18 closes with a verdict. Ibn Kathir explains that these are people who argue over whether it will happen at all and think it unlikely ever to come, and that "in error far away" means they are plainly ignorant. Why ignorant rather than merely mistaken? Because **the One who created the heavens and the earth is all the more able to give life to the dead.** He cites: "And He it is Who originates the creation, then He will repeat it; and this is easier for Him" (30:27).

The denial is not sophisticated. It is a failure to follow one's own reasoning to the end: a person who accepts that he was brought out of nothing once cannot coherently call it far-fetched that he be brought back.

## Ayah 19: the gentleness underneath it all

After a warning about wrath, a severe torment, and a Day that may be at the door, the passage turns — and the turn is the tenderest thing in it.

**"Allah is Laṭīf with His servants; He provides for whom He wills; and He is the All-Strong, the Almighty."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the word *laṭīf* carries more than one lexical meaning. **Ibn 'Abbas** rendered it here as *kind*; **'Ikrimah** rendered it as *benefactor*. Many meanings of *laṭīf* are gathered in the Tafsīr of Qurṭubī, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says all of them are covered by these two words: kind, and benefactor.

**Muqātil** pushed it further, in a comment that should stop us: Allah is kind to *all* His servants — so much so that even the disbelievers and the sinners keep on being showered with His worldly blessings. Ibn Kathir says the same in his own words: Allah provides for every last one of His creation and forgets no one; when it comes to His provision, **the righteous and the sinner are alike.** He cites: "And no moving creature is there on the earth but its provision is due from Allah. And He knows its dwelling place and its deposit. All is in a Clear Book" (11:6).

Sit with the placement. The ayah before this consigned the mockers to far-gone error. This ayah says He is still feeding them. A warning of wrath and severe torment does not switch off the daily generosity: the same Lord who has told these people exactly where their dispute leads is the One keeping them alive and provided for while they dispute.

**"He provides for whom He wills."** If provision reaches everyone, why does the ayah say *whom He wills*? Ibn Kathir reads it as generosity: He gives generously to whomever He wills. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers the question directly by way of Tafsīr Mazharī: there are countless kinds of sustenance. **Necessary** sustenance is provided to all and sundry without exception — even to creatures on land and in the waters whom nobody knows. But certain **special** kinds are distributed in degrees and quantities determined by His perfect wisdom: one person is given more wealth and goods, another more health and strength, another more learning and knowledge, another something else again.

And then the reason, which turns the whole verse into social insight: because provision is distributed unevenly, **everybody ends up dependent on somebody else** — and it is exactly this dependence that persuades people to cooperate with and help one another. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls that dependence the foundation of human civilization. The inequality you resent is the reason you need your neighbour, and he needs you.

**Ja'far ibn Muhammad** described Allah's kindness in the matter of sustenance as working in two ways (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān citing Mazharī and Qurṭubī). First, He provides every living being with food and other necessities according to its need. Second — and this is the subtle one — **He does not give anyone a lifetime's sustenance all at once**, but gives it gradually as the need arises, since otherwise preserving it would not even be feasible. Think of what a whole life's food delivered on one morning would mean. The daily drip we experience as insecurity is itself a mercy in the design.

**"And He is the All-Strong, the Almighty."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is one line: **there is nothing that can overpower Him.** Note how the ayah pairs the names. Gentleness and kindness (*Laṭīf*) sit beside irresistible power (*al-Qawiyy*, *al-'Azīz*), and each keeps the other from being misread. His kindness is not the indulgence of someone unable to enforce; His power is not the harshness of someone incapable of tenderness. This is also the answer to the whole passage: the Book and the Balance came from a Lord kind enough to send guidance, and the Hour is certain because that same Lord cannot be resisted.

## Living it

**Carry the Book and the Balance together.** If "truth" is Allah's right over you and "the Balance" is people's rights over one another, then a spirituality that leaves your dealings untouched has taken only half of what was sent down.

**Let the unknown date do its work.** Ibn Kathir said the question in ayah 17 was meant to spur striving, to warn, and to make you think little of this world. Whenever the thought of the Hour arises, redirect it as the Prophet ﷺ did — not *when*, but *what have I prepared*.

**Check which certainty you have.** Both groups in ayah 18 know the Hour is spoken of; only one group lets it change the calendar. Belief that produces no preparation sits closer to the mocker's position than we like to think.

**Guard your loves.** "You will be with those whom you love" makes love a form of preparation. Ask what your affections are attached to, because they are quietly booking your company.

**Trust the portioning.** Reading "He provides for whom He wills" through Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes the sting out of comparison. What you were given less of, someone else was given so that you would need him — and what you were given more of was given so that he would need you.

**A note on a reported practice.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records, from Shah 'Abdul Ghanī Phulpūrī relating from Hājī Imdādullāh, that whoever regularly recites this ayah — *Allāhu laṭīfun bi-'ibādihi yarzuqu man yashā'u wa huwa'l-Qawiyyu'l-'Azīz* — seventy times every morning would be preserved from shortage of sustenance, and that experience has shown this to be very effective. This is transmitted as the experience of later scholars, not as a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ; it is passed on here as the source itself passes it on.

passages.title: Sowing for the Hereafter and the reckoning of what is sown
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat sort humanity by one question: what is a person actually working for? The passage then asks who ever gave anyone the right to institute a religion, sets the two crowds of the Day of Resurrection side by side, and closes by naming the only "fee" the Prophet ﷺ ever asked of his people.

**What holds them together** is a single phrase that opens the passage and returns at its close: *nazid lahu*, "We give him increase." In ayah 20 Allah promises increase to whoever desires the Hereafter; in ayah 23, "whoever earns a good righteous deed, We shall give him an increase of good in respect thereof." Everything in between — the false legislators of ayah 21, the terrified wrongdoers of ayah 22 — shows the alternative.

Ibn Kathir reaches ayah 20 through the ayah just before it, and it is worth one sentence of run-up: Allah "provides for every last one of them and does not forget anyone," and **"when it comes to His provision, the righteous and the sinner are alike,"** as in "And no moving creature is there on the earth but its provision is due from Allah" (11:6). *Al-Qawiyy al-ʿAzīz*, "the All-Strong, the Almighty," he glosses simply: there is nothing that can overpower Him. So the passage opens with a Lord already feeding everyone, believer and rejecter alike — which is exactly why ayah 20 is so serious. Since the food comes either way, the real question is not *what will I get* but *what am I working for*.

## Ayah 20: two people, two things wanted

**"Whosoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, We give him increase in his reward, and whosoever desires the reward of this world, We give him thereof, and he has no portion in the Hereafter."**

The word rendered "reward" here is *ḥarth*, which is also translated "harvest." Ibn Kathir's gloss on "whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter" is plain and worth holding onto: **"whoever does things for the sake of the Hereafter."** The dividing line is not the outward act; it is what a person is doing it *for*.

Notice how carefully the two halves are *not* parallel:

- For the one who desires the Hereafter: **"We give him increase in his reward."** A promise, with growth built into it.
- For the one who desires this world: **"We give him thereof"** — *minhā*, some of it, a portion of the very thing he asked for. No increase. And then the closing line falls: **"he has no portion in the Hereafter."**

Ibn Kathir presses on that increase, and what he says is larger than a bigger payout: **"We will give him strength and help him to do what he wants to do, and We will increase it for him. So for every good, We will multiply it and give him between ten and seven hundred good rewards," as much as Allah wills.** The help comes in the doing, not only in the accounting. The one who turns toward the Hereafter is given strength to keep turning.

On the other side Ibn Kathir is more severe than a quick reading suggests. He is describing the one who strives for worldly gains **"and never pays any heed to the Hereafter at all"**: Allah will deny him the Hereafter, "and in this world, if He wills He will give to him and if He does not will, he will gain neither. So the one who strives with this intention in mind will have the worst deal in this world and in the Hereafter." Even the worldly return he set his heart on is not guaranteed to him.

As proof that this is the Qur'an's settled position, Ibn Kathir brings the passage from Sūrat al-Isrāʾ: "Whoever desires the quick-passing, We readily grant him what We will for whom We like. Then, afterwards, We have appointed for him Hell… And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it, with the necessary effort due for it while he is a believer — then such are the ones whose striving shall be appreciated" (17:18–21). Three things sit in that second half: desire, effort worthy of what is desired, and faith. Wanting the Hereafter is not a mood; it is a striving that costs something.

## The sharpest warning: the right deed for the wrong purpose

The danger in ayah 20 is not only that a person might chase this world with worldly deeds, but that he might chase it *with the deeds of the Hereafter*. Ibn Kathir reports that Ubayy ibn Kaʿb (may Allah be pleased with him) said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"Give the glad tidings to this Ummah of sublimity, high status, victory and power in the land. But whoever among them does the deeds of the Hereafter for the sake of worldly gain, will have no portion of the Hereafter."** (Ibn Kathir reports this without naming a collection, so it is given here as he gives it.)

Note how the two halves are joined: the good news of honour and establishment in the land is real — and the very same worldly success is where the danger lies. The deed can look identical from outside; the difference is what is wanted from it. And the verdict is the same as for the open worldling: **no portion in the Hereafter.**

## Ayah 21: who gave them the right to institute a religion?

**"Or have they partners with Allah who have instituted for them a religion which Allah has not ordained?"**

Having exposed a corrupt intention, the passage turns to a corrupt authority. Ibn Kathir explains: **they do not follow what Allah has ordained of upright religion; on the contrary, they follow what their devils (*Shayāṭīn*), of men and jinn, have prescribed for them.** He gives the Arabian examples — the taboo livestock categories the pagans invented, *Baḥīrah*, *Sāʾibah*, *Waṣīlah* and *Ḥām*, animals set aside on nobody's authority but their own — and notes that they also permitted what Allah forbade: eating the flesh and blood of animals not slaughtered for consumption, and gambling, "and other kinds of misguidance, ignorance and falsehood." These were things they invented during the *Jāhiliyyah* — the age of ignorance before Islam — "when they came up with all kinds of false rulings on what was permitted and what was forbidden, and false rites of worship and other corrupt ideas."

That is the force of the rhetorical question, and Ibn Kathir's own heading for the section states it without softening: **making legislation for the creatures is shirk** — shirk being the association of partners with Allah, the one sin that puts a person outside faith. To declare things permitted and forbidden in religion, without Allah's permission, is not a minor error of jurisprudence in his reading; it is taking up something that belongs to Allah alone.

To show how gravely this is taken, Ibn Kathir cites what **"was recorded in the Sahih"** — that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, **"I saw ʿAmr ibn Luḥayy ibn Qamaʿah dragging his intestines in Hell"** — because he had been the first one to introduce the idea of the *Sāʾibah*. He was one of the kings of the Khuzāʿah tribe, and he was the one who had made the Quraysh worship idols. Note the weight of that: a man long dead is seen in punishment for being the one who *started* a false law that generations after him simply inherited.

**"And had it not been for a decisive Word, the matter would have been judged between them."** Ibn Kathir: the punishment would have been hastened for them, **were it not for the fact that it had already been decreed that it would be delayed until the Day of Resurrection.** The delay is not the absence of a verdict; it is a Word already spoken, fixing the reckoning at an appointed hour. **"And verily, for the wrongdoers there is a painful torment"** — Ibn Kathir: an agonising torment in Hell, what a terrible destination.

## Ayah 22: the two crowds, seen at once

**"You will see the wrongdoers fearful of that which they have earned, and it will surely befall them. But those who believe and do righteous deeds (will be) in the flowering meadows of the Gardens. They shall have whatsoever they desire with their Lord. That is the supreme grace."**

Ibn Kathir places the scene precisely: **in the arena of Resurrection.** And he catches what makes it terrible — they are fearful **of what they have earned.** Their terror is not of an external enemy but of their own record. **"And it will surely befall them"** — Ibn Kathir: the thing that they fear will undoubtedly happen to them; **"this is how they will be on the Day of Resurrection; they will be in a state of utter fear and terror."** In this world, dread is often worse than the outcome that follows it. There, the dread is an accurate preview.

Set against them, in the same breath, are those in *rawḍāt al-jannāt*, **"the flowering meadows of the Gardens,"** with an open-ended promise: **"they shall have whatsoever they desire with their Lord."**

Ibn Kathir lets the contrast do its work: **what comparison can there be between the former and the latter?** How can the one who will be in the arena of Resurrection in a state of humiliation and fear, deserving it for his own wrongdoing, be compared with the one in the gardens of Paradise, enjoying whatever he wants of food, drink, clothing, dwellings, scenery, spouses and other delights **"such as no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and has never crossed the minds of men"**? **"That is the supreme grace"** — Ibn Kathir: the ultimate victory and complete blessing.

## Ayah 23: the glad tidings, and a Messenger who charges nothing

**"That is whereof Allah gives glad tidings to His servants who believe and do righteous good deeds."**

Ibn Kathir's comment is short and steadying: **this will undoubtedly come to them, because it is glad tidings from Allah to them.** A promise is as certain as the One making it.

Then the ayah turns, and the placement rewards a pause. Ayah 21 was about people who instituted a religion for others without Allah's permission. Now the true Messenger ﷺ is told to state his price:

**"Say: 'No reward do I ask of you for this except to be kind to me for my kinship with you.'"**

Ibn Kathir explains this as the Prophet ﷺ addressing the idolaters among the disbelievers of Quraysh: *I do not ask you for anything in return for this message and sincere advice which I bring to you. All I ask is that you withhold your evil from me and let me convey the Messages of my Lord. If you will not help me, then do not disturb me, for the sake of the ties of kinship that exist between you and I.*

His decisive evidence is a report **recorded by Al-Bukhari**: Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) was asked about this ayah, and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said, "To be kind to the family of Muhammad." Ibn ʿAbbās said, **"No, you have jumped to a hasty conclusion. There was no clan among Quraysh to whom the Prophet ﷺ did not have some ties of kinship."** The meaning, he said, is: *except that you uphold the ties of kinship that exist between me and you.* Ibn Kathir notes it was also recorded by Imam Ahmad with a different chain of narration.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same reading as the explanation "adopted by most of the exegetes," and fills in the reasoning: the Prophet's ﷺ real right over Quraysh was that he is the Messenger of Allah and should be believed and obeyed — but even if they refused that, there remained a right they could not deny, since he was related to most of their tribes, and they themselves did not deny the rights of relatives.

There is a fine point of language here. Honouring kinship was already **their own obligation**, so it could not be taken as compensation for his preaching at all.
