Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that "except" is used in its idiomatic sense: *although, in reality, it is no compensation — and if you consider it to be so, that is your own mistake — in fact I do not charge any fee at all.* Every prophet in every age openly told his people that he asked no payment for his efforts and that his compensation lay with Allah alone; how then could the chief of all the prophets ﷺ ask a fee of his people?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this explanation is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) in the *Sahih of Bukhari* and the *Sahih of Muslim*, and that Mujāhid, Qatādah and a very large group of leading exegetes also adopted it. It adds the incident of Imam Shaʿbī, who was questioned about this ayah, wrote to Ibn ʿAbbās for the correct explanation, and received the same answer as above — related by Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Saʿd, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ḥākim and Bayhaqī, and certified by Ḥākim to be correct.

## Where the reports differ — and where the ummah does not

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the other narration too, **reported with a weak chain of reporters**: that when this ayah was revealed, people asked the Prophet ﷺ who his kinsfolk were, and he replied ʿAlī, Fāṭimah and their offspring (may Allah be pleased with them). Its authenticity **was considered weak by Suyūṭī in *Ad-Dur al-Manthūr* and by Ḥāfiẓ Ibn Ḥajar in his *takhrīj* — his tracing of the sources and chains — of the ahadith of *al-Kashshāf*.** On that narration the meaning would be that the only compensation the Prophet ﷺ asked of the ummah for his services was that they take care of his progeny — which, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, obviously does not befit the high stature of the prophets, and especially his ﷺ. So the correct and preferred explanation, generally favoured by the ummah, is the first one.

But that conclusion is about *what the ayah asks as a fee*, not about the standing of the Prophet's ﷺ family, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is emphatic about the difference. Only a misguided person would take it as diminishing them. A person's being a Muslim depends on having reverence and love for the Prophet ﷺ more than for anyone else in the whole universe, and the natural consequence of that love is reverence and love for those close to him, according to the degree of their closeness — his children being the closest, love for them is undoubtedly a necessary element of faith. And this does not mean forgetting his pure wives or the noble Companions (may Allah be pleased with them all), who had their own manifold closeness to him ﷺ.

**Love for the family and progeny of the Prophet ﷺ "has never been a matter of controversy in the ummah"** — it has been taken by the entire ummah unanimously as an essential requirement of faith. Controversies arise, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, when the reverence of others is attacked. Otherwise reverence and love even for the common descendants of the Prophet ﷺ, known as the *sādāt* — his descendants generally, however distantly related — is an honour for a Muslim and a source of reward in the Hereafter. Because many people had begun neglecting this, Imam al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah have mercy on him) denounced that attitude in a few couplets: calling out to the pilgrims streaming in waves toward Minā that **"if only the love of the progeny of the Holy Prophet ﷺ is *rafḍ* (extreme Shiʿism), then I ask all the jinn and humans of this universe to witness that I am also a *rāfiḍī* (staunch Shiʿah)."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this statement of Imam al-Shāfiʿī is in fact the standpoint of the whole ummah.

## The promise returns

The ayah closes by circling back to where the passage began:

**"And whoever earns a good righteous deed, We shall give him an increase of good in respect thereof. Verily, Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Ready to appreciate."**

The phrase is the same as in ayah 20 — *nazid lahu*, "We give him increase." What was said there of the whole is now said of the single deed. Ibn Kathir: **whoever does a good deed, We will increase him in good for it, i.e., in reward** — as in, "Surely, Allah wrongs not even of the weight of a speck of dust, but if there is any good, He doubles it, and gives from Him a great reward" (4:40).

The two names that close the ayah are exactly the two a struggling person needs. Ibn Kathir on *Ghafūr, Shakūr*: **He forgives many bad deeds and increases a small amount of good deeds; He conceals and forgives sins, and He multiplies and increases the reward of good deeds.** One name deals with the failures in the record; the other with the little that was managed.

## Living it

**Examine what you want, not only what you did.** The difference between the two people in ayah 20 is not how hard they worked, but which reward they *desired*. Ibn Kathir's gloss puts the test simply: is this being done "for the sake of the Hereafter"?

**Do not read worldly return as approval.** Allah provides for the righteous and the sinner alike, and gives the worldly striver a portion of what he asked for. Getting what you wanted is no evidence that you wanted the right thing.

**Guard religious deeds most carefully of all.** The report from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb warns about doing "the deeds of the Hereafter for the sake of worldly gain" — and it places that warning right beside the promise of honour and power in the land.

**Take nothing as religion without Allah's permission.** Ayah 21 puts declaring things permitted and forbidden outside human hands entirely; Ibn Kathir titles it plainly as shirk. Ask what a practice's authority is, not how old or established it feels — the rulings invented in the Jāhiliyyah felt settled and ancient to those who inherited them.

**Start small and expect increase.** A single good deed is met with "We give him increase" — and the two closing names promise that the same Lord covers what went wrong and enlarges the little that went right.

passages.title: The forgery charge, and the Lord who answers those who turn to Him
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat answer an accusation thrown at the Prophet ﷺ — that he fabricated the Qur'an — and then, having answered it, turn immediately to the door left open for the accusers themselves. What binds the passage together is a single movement: Allah defends His Messenger and His revelation (ayah 24), and in the very next breath describes Himself as the One who accepts repentance, pardons sins, and answers those who call on Him (ayat 25–26). The refutation is not the end of the conversation with the deniers; it is the beginning of an invitation.

## The setting: what comes just before

Ayah 23 has just given glad tidings of Paradise to "His servants who believe and do righteous good deeds," told the Prophet ﷺ to say he asks no reward for his message "except to be kind to me for my kinship with you," and promised that "whoever earns a good righteous deed, We shall give him an increase of good in respect thereof," closing with two of Allah's names: Oft-Forgiving, Most Ready to appreciate. Ibn Kathir unpacks those two names in a way that sets up everything that follows: He forgives many bad deeds and increases a small amount of good deeds; He conceals and forgives sins, and He multiplies and increases the reward of good deeds.

On the "kinship" phrase, Al-Bukhari recorded that Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) was asked about it. Sa'id bin Jubayr said it meant kindness to the family of Muhammad ﷺ. Ibn 'Abbas replied, "No, you have jumped to a hasty conclusion. There was no clan among Quraysh to whom the Prophet ﷺ did not have some ties of kinship" — the meaning being, "except that you uphold the ties of kinship that exist between me and you." Ibn Kathir notes that this was recorded by Al-Bukhari, and also by Imam Ahmad with a different chain of narration.

Ibn Kathir explains the sense of the ayah as an address to the idolators among the disbelievers of Quraysh: *I do not ask you for anything in return for this message and sincere advice which I bring to you. All I ask of you is that you withhold your evil from me and let me convey the Messages of my Lord. If you will not help me, then do not disturb me, for the sake of the ties of kinship that exist between you and I.* That is the mood in which ayah 24 lands. A man who has asked for nothing but to be left alone is then accused of inventing the whole thing.

## Ayah 24: "Or do they say, 'He has fabricated a lie about Allah'?"

The answer does not come as indignation. It comes as a condition:

**"If Allah willed, He could have sealed up your heart."**

Ibn Kathir reads it as a direct hypothetical addressed to the Prophet ﷺ: *if you had invented any lies against Him, as these ignorant people claim* — then Allah could seal up your heart, which Ibn Kathir glosses as: and thus caused you to forget what had already come to you of the Qur'an. The image is of a heart stamped shut, and of revelation already received slipping away.

Ibn Kathir sets alongside it the words of Sūrat al-Ḥāqqah: *"And if he had forged a false saying concerning Us, We surely would have seized him by his right hand, and then We certainly would have cut off his life artery, and none of you could have withheld Us from him"* (69:44–47) — which he glosses as: We would have wrought the utmost vengeance upon him, and no one among mankind would have been able to protect him. Put the two passages together and the logic is complete. Forging speech in Allah's name is not something a man is left free to keep doing.

### The rule behind the argument (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the principle the ayah is resting on. This first verse, it says, conveys Allah's reply to those who held the prophethood and messengership of the Prophet ﷺ to be false and the Qur'an to be wrong and forged. The reply rests on a divine rule: miracles — events occurring against the normal course of things, which ordinary human beings cannot perform — are created and shown through the prophets by Allah's grace, in order to prove their prophethood, and without any discretion of the prophets themselves. It is not a power they own.

What about magicians, who also perform strange feats? Maʿārif answers: neither the prophets nor the magicians can perform any of these things without Allah's intent and scheme. He allows the magicians their tricks as a measure of test and trial. But the rule He has laid down to distinguish magic from miracle, and a magician from a prophet, is this — **no false claimant of prophethood can perform any magical trick successfully.** Such tricks can be performed by a man right up until he claims prophethood; the magic vanishes as soon as he lays that false claim. And when Allah does bestow prophethood on someone, He favours him with miracles and makes those miracles highly visible, providing physical and decreed proof of his prophethood, and confirming him in His Divine Book.

Apply that rule to the Qur'an itself. Maʿārif points out that the Noble Qur'an is such a miracle that all the humans and all the jinn of this world are unable to produce even one verse comparable to a verse of the Qur'an. Their inability to do so was proved in the days of the Prophet ﷺ and continues till today. Such an open and obvious miracle cannot be accomplished by a false claimant of prophethood. The claim to *wahy* (revelation) and messengership is therefore correct and true, and those who hold it to be incorrect and forged are, in Maʿārif's words, misguided calumniators. Summed up in one line: **had there been — Allah forbid — something forged by the Prophet ﷺ in the Qur'an, Allah would have put a seal on his heart, and he would never have been able to come up with such a miraculous discourse.** And it is worth pausing on who is carrying it — Maʿārif opens by saying that the miraculous Qur'an recited by the unlettered Prophet ﷺ is in itself a clear proof of its being revealed by Allah.

### "And Allah wipes out falsehood, and establishes the truth by His Word"

The ayah does not stop at defending one man. Ibn Kathir explains "and establishes the truth by His Word" as: He establishes it and strengthens it and makes it clear by His Words — that is, by His evidence and His signs. Truth stands because Allah props it up with proof.

### "Verily, He knows well what is in the breasts"

The closing phrase turns the whole argument inward. Ibn Kathir: it means all that is hidden in the hearts of men. The accusers were speaking with their tongues; Allah is telling them He knows what is hidden underneath the words. It is also, quietly, the bridge into ayah 25 — as Ibn Kathir will say there, He knows all your deeds and actions and words, *and still* accepts the repentance of those who repent to Him.

## Ayah 25: the door that is still open

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads this ayah as an address to the deniers and opponents just spoken of: **there is still time.** Give up and renounce your disbelief and *kufr*; Allah is very merciful and Most Beneficent, He accepts the repentance of those who truly repent, and He forgives their sins. That is a startling turn. The people who called the Prophet ﷺ a forger are, one ayah later, being told the way back is open.

Ibn Kathir puts it as a reminder to His servants that He accepts repentance: if they turn to Him and come back to Him, then by His kindness and generosity He forgives, overlooks and conceals their sins — as in the ayah, *"And whoever does evil or wrongs himself but afterwards seeks Allah's forgiveness, he will find Allah Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful"* (4:110).

He explains the halves of the ayah precisely: **"and forgives sins"** means He will accept repentance in the future, and He forgives past sins. And **"and He knows what you do"** means He knows all your deeds and actions and words — *yet He still accepts the repentance of those who repent to Him*. The knowledge and the pardon sit in the same sentence.

### How pleased is Allah with a returning servant?

It was reported in **Sahih Muslim** that Anas bin Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Allah is more pleased with the repentance of His servant than anyone of you who loses his riding beast in a barren land, and it was carrying his food and drink; he despairs of ever finding it, so he comes to a tree and lies down in its shade, having given up all hope of finding his riding beast; then whilst he is there like that, suddenly he sees it standing near him, so he takes hold of its reins and because of his great joy he says, 'O Allah, You are my slave and I am Your Lord!'"

The last line is the point of the whole picture, and the hadith itself explains it: he makes a mistake because of his great joy. The man is so overcome that he garbles the sentence and gets Lord and servant the wrong way round. That is the *human* end of the comparison, and the Prophet ﷺ says Allah's pleasure at a servant's return is greater still.

Ibn Kathir adds that a similar report was also narrated in the Sahih from 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him). A further narration reported from Az-Zuhri, from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), gives the same image in a different key: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah rejoices more over the repentance of His servant than one of you feels when he finds his lost camel in a place where he had feared that he would die of thirst.

**A practical application from a Companion.** Hammam bin Al-Harith said that Ibn Mas'ud was asked about a man who commits immoral sins with a woman and then marries her. He said, "There is nothing wrong with that," and recited this very ayah: *"And He it is Who accepts repentance from His servants."*

### What repentance actually is (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān)

Because the ayah offers so much, Maʿārif is careful to define the term. The literal meaning of **taubah** is *to return and turn to* — the word itself is a picture of a person walking back. In religious terminology, giving up and renouncing any sin is called taubah. Maʿārif lists three conditions for it to be proper and genuine:

1. **Give up, immediately, the sin one is involved in.**
2. **Repent for the past sin.**
3. **Determine firmly not to commit it in future.**

Then the details that people usually skip:

- **If it pertains to neglect of an obligatory duty (fard)** — one has to start observing it, or start offering the prescribed compensation.
- **If it relates to the rights of another person, and that right is monetary or material** — if the person is alive, the money or property has to be returned to him, unless he agrees to forgo it. If he is not alive but his heirs are available, it goes to the heirs. If the heirs are also not available, it is deposited in the Islamic public treasury (*bait-ul-mal*); and if there is no public treasury, or it is not managed properly, it is given as alms on his behalf.
- **If the right owed is not monetary or material** — for example, if someone has been unduly distressed, or abused, or backbitten — then that person has to be pleased, and forgiveness has to be sought and obtained from him or her.

Two further points Maʿārif insists on. First, for all kinds of taubah, the giving up of sin must be **for the sake of Allah**, and not due to any physical inability or weakness. Stopping because you no longer can is not taubah. Second, the Sharī'ah demands that one ought to renounce *all* sins; but if someone renounces only a particular sin, Ahl-us-Sunnah hold that that particular sin would be forgiven, while his liability for other sins would continue. Partial repentance is real as far as it goes — it is simply not a general amnesty.

## Ayah 26: "And He answers those who believe and do righteous good deeds"

Ayah 25 was about Allah receiving what we bring to Him. Ayah 26 is about Allah giving back.

**"And He answers those who believe and do righteous good deeds."** As-Suddi said this means: He responds to them. Ibn Jarir held the same view and specified it — it means that He answers their supplication for themselves, their companions and their brothers. So the answered supplication is not narrowly self-serving; a believer's prayer for other people is part of what is answered.

Note the two qualifications the ayah itself attaches: **faith** and **righteous deeds**. The response is described as belonging to people whose lives are pointed in Allah's direction.

**"And gives them increase of His bounty."** Ibn Kathir: it means He answers their supplications and gives them more besides. This is the same generosity already announced in ayah 23 — *"whoever earns a good righteous deed, We shall give him an increase of good in respect thereof"* — which Ibn Kathir there glosses as: whoever does a good deed, We will increase him in good for it, in reward. And it is the meaning of the ayah he cites alongside it: *"Surely, Allah wrongs not even the weight of a speck of dust, but if there is any good, He doubles it, and gives from Him a great reward"* (4:40).

**An early reading of "increase."** Qatadah, narrating from Ibrahim An-Nakha'i Al-Lakhmi, took the ayah to a further horizon: "And He answers those who believe and do righteous good deeds" means they intercede for their brothers; "and gives them increase of His bounty" means they intercede for their brothers' brothers.

**And the other side.** The ayah ends with the counterweight: *and as for the disbelievers, theirs will be a severe torment.* Ibn Kathir observes the deliberate pairing — having mentioned the believers and the great reward that is theirs, Allah then mentions the disbelievers and the severe, painful, agonizing torment that they will find with Him on the Day of Resurrection, the Day when they are brought to account. The invitation of ayah 25 is real, and so is the cost of refusing it.

## Living it

**Look at the Book itself.** Ayah 24 answers the charge of forgery by pointing at what is in front of the accusers. As Maʿārif puts it, the inability of all humans and all jinn to produce even one comparable verse was proved in the days of the Prophet ﷺ and continues till today.

**Do not let the size of a sin argue you out of returning.** The people addressed here had called a prophet a forger, and Maʿārif reads the next ayah as telling them there is still time. Ibn Kathir's gloss keeps the two halves together: He knows all your deeds and actions and words — and still accepts the repentance of those who repent to Him.

**Repent properly, not vaguely.** Give the sin up now, repent for what is past, resolve firmly against returning to it — and settle what you owe people: money or property back to its owner or his heirs, and pardon sought and obtained where the harm was not material. And do it for the sake of Allah, not because you have simply become unable to sin.

**Make supplication (du'a) as a believer, and pray for others.** Ayah 26 ties the answer to faith and righteous action, and Ibn Jarir extends it explicitly to supplication for one's companions and brothers. Then leave room for the extra: Ibn Kathir says He answers their supplications *and gives them more besides*.

passages.title: Provision measured, rain after despair, creation as sign
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat answer a question that lives in almost every believing heart: if Allah truly answers those who call on Him, why am I not given what I ask for — and why do the people who ignore Him seem to have so much? The passage replies not with a rebuke but with a tour of Allah's governance of the world: provision sent down by measure (ayah 27), rain withheld until hope is gone and then poured out (ayah 28), and the heavens and earth filled with creatures He is able to assemble whenever He wills (ayah 29). What holds the three together, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, is that they are a single proof of Allah's Oneness drawn from the perfection of His wisdom: the universe is tied together by a stable system, and that system is supervised by a Being who is All-Wise and All-Aware.

## The question these ayat answer

The ayah just before this passage said that Allah answers those who believe and do righteous deeds and gives them increase of His bounty. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that a person can be genuinely perplexed here: a Muslim supplicates for some worldly need, and his objective is not met. Ayah 27 removes the confusion. Sometimes the fulfilment of all of a person's desires is in neither his own interest nor his society's. So if a supplication has apparently not been accepted, that too is for the sake of a greater well-being of the universe which nobody knows except the All-Knowing, All-Wise Creator. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the underlying point, citing Tafsīr Kabīr: if every human being of this world were given every kind of sustenance and every kind of blessing, this system of the world simply could not be managed wisely.

**The occasion of revelation.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that some narrations corroborate that this ayah was revealed about those Muslims who used to wish that they too should get the same wealth and opulence that was available to the disbelievers. Imam Baghawi (may Allah have mercy on him) reproduces the statement of Khabbab ibn al-Aratt (may Allah be pleased with him) that when they saw the wealth and opulence of Banu Qurayzah, Banu Nadir and Banu Qaynuqaʿ — which the source identifies as Jewish tribes — the desire to have such affluence welled up in their hearts also, and thereafter this ayah was revealed. And ʿAmr ibn Harith (may Allah be pleased with him) states that some of the Companions known as the people of the Suffah — the source names them by that title — had expressed to the Prophet ﷺ their desire that Allah would make them wealthy, and this ayah was revealed thereafter. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives its source for this second report as Ruh al-Maʿani and other works.)

Sit with that for a moment. The people being addressed are not the greedy and the heedless. They are believers who asked to be made wealthy — which is to say, people who did not have wealth. The ayah does not shame them. It lifts their eyes to how the whole system works.

## Ayah 27: "And if Allah were to extend the provision for His servants…"

Ibn Kathir renders the ayah: *And if Allah were to extend the provision for His servants, they would surely rebel in the earth, but He sends down by measure as He wills. Verily, He is, in respect of His servants, the Well-Aware, the All-Seer.* The condition is not merely "if He gave them provision" but if He *extended* it — abundant provision, as the passage translation has it, for all His servants at once.

And the answer: *they would surely rebel in the earth.* Ibn Kathir explains the meaning as: if We gave them more provision than they need, this would make them rebel and transgress against one another in an arrogant and insolent manner.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the mechanism up. Had every kind of sustenance and every kind of blessing been provided abundantly to every individual of this world, the discord and dispute between one another would have crossed all limits — because in such abundance nobody would be in need of another person, nor would one be subdued by another. And wealth has this quality: greed and inordinate desire increase with the increase in wealth. The result would necessarily have been the common use of force to take possession of another person's property, and so disputes and fights, rebellion and other misdeeds beyond all limits.

**So what did Allah do instead?** He distributed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the pattern: somebody has abundance of riches and wealth, another person is healthier and stronger, another is more comely and beautiful, and yet another has surpassed others in knowledge and wisdom. In short, everybody is dependent on others for one thing or another — "and it is this inter-dependence which is the foundation of civilization." The unevenness you resent is the thing that holds human society together.

**"But He sends down by measure as He wills."** Not without limit, then, but in due measure. Ibn Kathir: He gives them provision according to what is in their best interests, and He knows best about that; so He makes rich those who deserve to be rich, and He makes poor those who deserve to be poor. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the same conclusion — that Allah has bestowed His blessings upon the people of this world in a special way, measured rather than uniform.

**"Verily, He is, in respect of His servants, the Well-Aware, the All-Seer."** Two of Allah's names close the ayah — *al-Khabīr*, the Well-Aware, and *al-Baṣīr*, the All-Seer. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads them here as the seal on the whole argument: by them it is indicated that Allah knows very well what is good for a person and what is harmful. Accordingly He has provided everybody with what is good for him, and if He has deprived somebody of anything, it is because of that person's welfare and the welfare of the whole world.

**The limits of our vision.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful here, and this is worth carrying with you: it is *not at all necessary* that we should understand the underlying wisdom and welfare behind the decision about every individual, because everyone thinks on the basis of his own limited knowledge, whereas Allah is looking at the whole world. The illustration given is of an honest head of state whose orders happen to affect some people adversely. The person so affected is quite likely to feel bad about those orders, because his thinking is limited to his own interest. But a person who is looking at the circumstances of the whole state and the whole nation — and who appreciates that the whole state cannot be sacrificed for the sake of one individual's interest — does not consider such a step to be bad. Then how is it possible to gauge the wisdom of the Being who is managing the system of the whole universe? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes that if this point is kept in mind, the confusion and perplexity generated by the sight of anyone surrounded by tribulation would disappear by itself.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also draws a further conclusion from the ayah: the distribution of wealth and goods equally to all the people of the world is neither possible, nor desirable, nor required for the existence of the system of the universe — with the detailed discussion deferred to its commentary on Sūrah al-Zukhruf 43:32.

**But Paradise has abundance without corruption — why?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious question: all kinds of blessings will be provided in abundance to all human beings in Paradise, so why would that not cause mischief there? The answer: the cause of mischief in this world is abundance of wealth and goods *coupled with* greed and the inordinate desire for more that keeps increasing along with wealth. In Paradise that greed and inordinate desire will simply not be there, although blessings and delights will keep on being showered. And to the follow-up — why not remove greed here too, and then provide abundance in this world as well? — the answer is that the very purpose of creating this world is to have the co-existence of good and evil; without that it is simply not possible to arrange the trial of human beings, which is the real purpose of the creation of the universe. Strip greed and desire out of human beings altogether and the real purpose of this world would have failed. Paradise, on the other hand, comprises goodness only, so such base emotions will simply not be there.

## Ayah 28: rain after hope is gone

**"And He it is Who sends down the rain after they have despaired, and spreads His mercy."**

Ibn Kathir explains: after the people have given up hope that rain will fall, He sends it down upon them at their time of need. He points to the parallel in Sūrah al-Rum: "And verily, before that — just before it was sent down upon them — they were in despair!" (30:49).

**Why the delay?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the most searching treatment here. It is usual for Allah to send down rain whenever the earth is in severe need of water. But the words "after they have lost hope" draw attention to something else: sometimes, in deviation from His usual norm, Allah delays sending down rain so much that people begin losing hope. Apart from trial, such a happening is a warning — that rain and famine are all in the power of Allah. Whenever He wills He stops the rain because of people's misdeeds, so that people turn their attention towards His kindness and display their humility and their dependence. And there is a further reason: if rains had been subject to a strict timetable without any deviation, people would have considered rain to be purely subject to apparent causes, and would have become inattentive to Allah's power. The break in the pattern is what keeps the heart awake.

**A crucial clarification.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stops to define the despair the ayah describes: here losing hope means losing hope in their own contrivances — their means, their arrangements — because disappointment with Allah's kindness is *kufr*, disbelief. This is the difference between a believer at the end of his resources and a believer at the end of his hope. The first is exactly where the ayah finds people just before the mercy arrives. The second is a state a believer must never enter.

**"And spreads His mercy."** Ibn Kathir: He bestows it upon all the people who live in that region. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point when it sums the passage up — the good things of the universe which are of general benefit have been provided to everyone. Wealth is apportioned; rain falls on the whole region.

**ʿUmar and the rain.** Ibn Kathir records from Qatadah: it was mentioned to them that a man said to ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), "O Commander of the faithful, no rain has come and the people are in despair." ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) replied simply, "Rain will be sent upon you" — and recited this very ayah. That is what it looks like when a person's certainty is anchored in the Book: the ayah itself was his forecast.

**"And He is the Protector, Worthy of all praise."** Ibn Kathir explains the pair together: He is the One who is in control of His creation, taking care of what will benefit them in this world and the Hereafter, and the consequences of all His decrees and actions are good, for which He is worthy of all praise. That is the answer to the whole complaint the passage began with: Allah is not merely in control of your situation, He is taking care of what benefits you in it, and every one of His decrees terminates in something praiseworthy.

## Ayah 29: the sign that is everything around you

**"And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and whatever moving creatures He has dispersed in them both."**

*Among His signs* — Ibn Kathir glosses these as the signs which point to His great might and power. The argument has moved outward: from your provision, to your region's rainfall, to the entire cosmos. "Whatever He has dispersed in them both" means, Ibn Kathir says, whatever He has created in them — that is, in the heavens and the earth.

**"Moving creatures" — dābbah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the original lexical meaning of *dābbah*, the word translated as "creatures," is anything which moves about of its own will; only later did the word come to be used for animals. So the ayah is not simply about livestock. Ibn Kathir's list is expansive: this includes the angels, men, jinn and all the animals with their different shapes, colours, languages, natures, kinds and types — and He has distributed them throughout the various regions of the heavens and the earth. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the creatures which move about on the earth are all too visible; the ones which move about in the sky could well be the angels, and it is quite possible that there may be some creatures in the sky so far unknown to man.

**"And He is Able to assemble them whenever He wills."** Ibn Kathir marks the force of the "and He" — meaning, yet despite all of that. This gathering is the Day of Resurrection: He will gather the first and the last of them, and bring all His creatures together in one place where they will all hear the voice of the caller and all of them will be seen clearly; then He will judge between them with justice and truth. The One who can disperse creation this widely across the heavens and the earth and then call every last one of it back to a single standing ground is not a Lord whose measuring out of your provision you need to second-guess.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes the passage with a summary worth taking whole. In view of the system of the universe, Allah has not provided everyone with wealth and goods in abundance; rather He has distributed them in accordance with the dictates of wisdom. But the good things of the universe which are of general benefit have been provided to everyone — rain, clouds, earth, sky and the creatures in them have all been created for the benefit of human beings, and they all demonstrate the Oneness of Allah.

So the passage asks four things of a believer:

**Stop reading your income as a verdict.** Ayah 27 says the measure is set by One who is, in respect of His servants, the Well-Aware and the All-Seer — set, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, by what is actually good for you and for the whole world.

**Look for the share you were given.** If the wisdom is that each person is rich in something and needy in something else — wealth, health, strength, beauty, knowledge and wisdom — then your task is to find and use what you were handed, not to audit what someone else was handed.

**Do not confuse the end of your means with the end of hope.** Ayah 28 shows Allah deliberately delaying until human calculation has run out. Losing hope in your own contrivances is where the rain begins; disappointment with Allah's kindness, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān warns, is disbelief.

**Turn the complaint inward.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's final word on the passage: if after all this anyone suffers any hardship, he should consider it to be due to his own deeds, and he should do a little heart-searching, instead of complaining against Allah.

And the last note is not severity but comfort. The One measuring out your provision is the Protector, Worthy of all praise — taking care of what will benefit you in this world and the Hereafter, and the consequences of everything He decrees are good.

passages.title: What your own hands earn, on land and at sea
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These six ayat take a single truth and show it in two settings: the hardships that strike us are tied to what our own hands have earned, and even so, Allah forgives far more than He calls to account. Ayat 30–31 say this on land, about you and me; ayat 32–35 say it at sea, about ships that ride the water only because Allah holds the wind steady for them. What binds the passage together is one repeated sentence — **"and He pardons much"** — which lands once in ayah 30 and again in ayah 34, and one repeated warning: there is nowhere to escape to (ayah 31: you cannot escape Him in the earth; ayah 35: those who dispute Our signs have no place of refuge).

## Ayah 30: "because of what your own hands have earned"

Ibn Kathir explains this plainly: whatever disasters happen to you, O mankind, are because of sins you have committed in the past. The verse does not describe hardship as random weather. It links what strikes a person to something real in that person's record.

But notice how the sentence ends before you have finished absorbing the first half: **"and He pardons much."** Ibn Kathir reads this as forgiveness of sins — He does not punish you for them; rather He forgives you. Read the ayah again with both halves held together and the emphasis shifts. Whatever hardship you have tasted is less than what your record could have produced. Ibn Kathir brings a verse from elsewhere in the Qur'an to make the point unmistakable: if Allah were to punish men for that which they earned, He would not leave a moving creature on the surface of the earth (35:45). The fact that anyone is still standing is itself an argument for how much is being overlooked.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes a narration from Sayyidnā Ḥasan (may Allah be pleased with him) that when this verse was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ said: "I swear by the Being Who holds my life, that anyone who gets scratched by a piece of wood, or his nerve shivers or his step falters is all due to his sins, and Allah Taʿālā does not punish for every sin, rather the number of sins He overlooks far exceeds those for which any punishment is given." (Maʿārif reports this without naming a hadith collection for it, so take it as the commentary transmits it.)

That last clause is the mood of the whole passage. The scale is not tipped toward reckoning. It is tipped, heavily, toward pardon.

## The mercy hidden inside the hardship

Ibn Kathir then does something important. Having established that trouble is connected to sin, he shows what that connection actually means for a believer — and it turns out to be a mercy rather than a bill.

He cites, as a rigorously authentic (*ṣaḥīḥ*) hadith, these words of the Prophet ﷺ — an oath sworn on his own life: "By the One in Whose Hand is my soul, no believer is stricken with fatigue, exhaustion, worry or grief, but Allah will forgive him for some of his sins thereby — even a thorn which pricks him." (Ibn Kathir grades it ṣaḥīḥ but does not name the collection at this point, so we take the teaching as he gives it without attaching a source to it.)

Then two narrations he attributes to **Imam Ahmad**:

- From Muʿāwiyah ibn Abī Sufyān (may Allah be pleased with him), who said he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "No physical harm befalls a believer, but Allah will expiate for some of his sins because of it."
- From ʿĀ'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), who reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "If a person commits many sins and has nothing that will expiate for them, Allah will test him with some grief that will expiate for them."

Put these beside ayah 30 and the logic completes itself. The hardship is not the debt being collected; it is the debt being *cleared*. The thorn is not the punishment your sins deserved — it is the merciful token that stands in place of it. And the ʿĀ'ishah narration adds a striking possibility: for someone whose sins have piled up with nothing to wipe them away, a sorrow may be sent precisely so that something *does*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān seals this with a narration recorded, it says, by **Ḥākim in the Mustadrak** and by **Baghawī**, on the authority of Sayyidnā ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him): sins for which punishment is given in this world are forgiven for Muslims in the Hereafter (cited via Maẓharī). Nothing is charged twice.

## Who this verse is addressing — an important caution

Before anyone turns this ayah into a weapon, the scholars themselves fence it in. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from **Baiḍāwī and others** that the verse is specifically meant for those people who are likely to commit sins. The hardships and troubles that befall prophets — who are innocent of sins — and children who have not reached the age of puberty, and those who are not in their right mind, are *not* covered by this verse. There are other reasons for their trials: for example, that they are upgraded in their rewards. And Maʿārif adds the honest limit: in reality a man cannot fathom the depths of the wisdom behind them. Allah knows best.

This is how the verse is meant to be used. Turn it on yourself, where it produces repentance. Do not turn it on the suffering person in front of you, where it produces only cruelty and a claim to knowledge you do not have.

## Sin's other punishment: more sin

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes **Maulānā Ashraf ʿAlī Thānavī** (may Allah have mercy on him) making the reach of the verse wider than bodily pain: just as physical hardships and tortures befall due to sins, the inner ailments are also caused by sins — and one sin committed by a person becomes the cause for getting involved in other sins.

Alongside this, Maʿārif cites **Ḥāfiẓ Ibn al-Qayyim** in his book *Ad-Dawāʾ ush-Shāfī*: one prompt punishment of a sin is that one gets involved in other sins; and, in the same way, the prompt reward of a virtuous deed is that it attracts another virtue.

That is a sobering and a hopeful thought at once. Sin's first penalty is not lightning; it is the next sin, arriving more easily than the last. And obedience's first reward is not a distant prize; it is the next act of obedience, arriving more easily than the last. Whichever direction you are moving in, it is already paying you in its own currency.

## Ayah 31: nowhere to run, no one else to run to

"And you cannot escape from Allah in the earth, and besides Allah you have neither any protector nor any helper." Two doors are shut in one sentence. You cannot outrun Him — the earth offers no distance great enough. And you cannot be shielded from Him by anyone else, because outside of Him there is no protecting friend and no helper at all.

This is what makes ayah 30 urgent rather than merely interesting. If misfortune is tied to what our hands earn, and there is no jurisdiction outside His reach and no patron to intervene, then the only sane move is the one the ayah pushes you toward: turn back to the very One in whose hand it all is.

## Ayat 32–33: ships like mountains, and a wind that could simply stop

Now the passage moves out onto the water — and the argument is made again, in a form anyone in a trading city could picture.

Ibn Kathir: another sign of Allah's great power and dominion is the fact that He has subjugated the sea so that ships may sail in it by His command, so they sail in the sea like mountains. This comparison was the view of **Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, as-Suddī and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk** — in other words, these ships on the sea are like mountains on land. Something enormous, immovable-looking, a landmark — and it is *floating*.

Then ayah 33 removes one small thing: "If He wills, He causes the wind to cease, then they would become motionless on the surface of the sea." Ibn Kathir: these are the winds that cause the ships to travel on the sea; if He willed, He could cause them to cease, then the ships would not move and would remain still, neither coming nor going, staying where they are on the surface of the water. Not sunk. Not smashed. Simply *stopped*. The mountain that crosses oceans is undone by the absence of a breeze it never owned.

And the ayah says these are signs **"for everyone patient and grateful"** — *ṣabbār shakūr*. Ibn Kathir separates the two words and assigns each its moment: patient means patient in the face of adversity, at times of difficulty; grateful means grateful at times of ease. He then points out where the blessing lies in the first place — that Allah subjugated the sea and sends as much wind as they need in order to travel; in that there are signs of His blessings to His creation. So the sign is legible to a certain kind of person: one who holds steady when the wind dies, and thanks Allah when it fills the sail. Anyone who only ever does one of the two will read half of reality and miss the other half.

## Ayah 34: "or He may destroy them" — and again, "He pardons much"

Ibn Kathir: if He wills, He may destroy the ships and drown them, because of the sins of the people on board. Some of the scholars interpreted the phrase *yūbiqhunna* differently — that if He willed, He could send the wind to blow fiercely so that it would take the ships and divert them from their courses, driving them to the right or the left, so that they would be lost and would not be able to follow their intended path. Ibn Kathir notes that this reading also includes the idea of their being destroyed, and that it fits the first meaning: still the wind and they stop dead; unleash the wind and they are lost. Two opposite catastrophes, both a hair's breadth away, both withheld.

Then the refrain returns: **"and He pardons much."** Ibn Kathir's comment here is the sharpest line in the passage — if He were to punish them for all of their sins, He would destroy everyone who sails on the sea. Nobody would ever make port.

And he draws out the principle behind the restraint: by His grace and mercy He sends the wind *according to their needs*, just as He sends rain that is sufficient. If He sent too much rain, it would destroy their houses; if He sent too little, their crops and fruits would not grow. He even gives a worked example: in the case of lands such as Egypt, He sends water from another land, because they do not need rain — if rain were to fall upon them, it would destroy their houses and cause walls to collapse.

This is the quiet centre of the whole passage. Everything that keeps you alive is calibrated — the wind at the strength that carries rather than capsizes, the rain in the amount that grows rather than destroys, the reckoning at the level that corrects rather than annihilates. The mercy is not only in what Allah gives; it is in the *measure* He gives it in.

## Ayah 35: "no place of refuge"

The passage closes on those who dispute Allah's signs. Ibn Kathir: they have no means of escape from His torment and vengeance, for they are subdued by His power.

It is a deliberate echo of ayah 31 — you cannot escape from Allah in the earth — and it explains why the whole sea-image was raised at all. A man standing on a deck arguing against the signs of his Lord is being carried by a wind he did not make, over a sea he did not subdue, on a hull that would sit dead in the water at a word. Ayah 35 simply asks him to notice.

## Living it

**When something strikes you, look inward first, not outward.** Ayah 30 puts the question "what have my hands earned?" before the question "who did this to me?" That is not despair; it is the only version of the question you can actually act on.

**Read hardship as expiation, not as rejection.** On the narrations Ibn Kathir cites, a believer's fatigue, exhaustion, worry, grief — down to a thorn's prick — clear away sins. And on the report Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits from Sayyidnā ʿAlī, what is settled here is not raised again there.

**Never use this ayah on someone else.** Baiḍāwī and those with him ruled out prophets, children before puberty and those not of sound mind from its scope, and Maʿārif admits outright that the wisdom behind a given trial is beyond us. Judgement of another person's suffering is exactly the knowledge we were told we do not have.

**Watch the small drift.** On Ibn al-Qayyim's point as Maʿārif cites it, a sin's prompt punishment is getting involved in further sins, and a good deed's prompt reward is that it attracts another good deed. Do not wait for a catastrophe to tell you which way you are pointed; look at what came easily to you today.

**Be *ṣabbār shakūr* — both.** Patient when the wind stops; grateful when it blows. Ayah 33 says the signs are there for that person specifically. The one who is only patient sees hardship everywhere; the one who is only grateful collapses at the first stillness. The believer the Qur'an describes here is the one who can read both the calm and the crossing as coming from the same measured, merciful hand.

**And whenever you tally what has gone wrong in your life, put the refrain beside it.** He pardons much. Twice in six ayat, and by Ibn Kathir's reckoning, so much that the sea still carries ships and the earth still carries us.

passages.title: What is with Allah is better: the believers' traits
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat make one argument. Ayah 36 gives the verdict on everything a person can be handed in this world — a passing enjoyment, while "that which is with Allah is better and more lasting." Then the passage names the people for whom that lasting thing is reserved, describing them by their habits. Ibn Kathir titles the section exactly that way — "The Attributes of Those Who deserve that which is with Allah."

## Ayah 36: the honest price of everything you own

**"So whatever you have been given is but (a passing) enjoyment for this worldly life."** Ibn Kathir draws out the warning inside the phrasing: *no matter what you achieve and amass, do not be deceived by it*. The Arabic calls it *matāʿ al-ḥayāt al-dunyā* — the enjoyment of *al-dunyā*, which Ibn Kathir glosses as "the lower, transient realm that will undoubtedly come to an end." The verse does not say the world's goods are evil. It says they are *given*, and that they are real enjoyment — of a realm that has an end built into it.

**"But that which is with Allah is better and more lasting."** Two claims, not one: *better* in quality, *more lasting* (*abqā*) in duration. Ibn Kathir's conclusion is plain arithmetic: "the reward of Allah is better than this world, and it will last forever, so do not give preference to that which is transient over that which is lasting." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames the passage the same way: these verses "state the imperfection and temporary nature of the blessings of this world, as against the perfection and permanence of the blessings of the Hereafter."

**Who is it for?** The sentence continues: *for those who believe and put their trust in their Lord*. Faith is the first and indispensable condition — "without which nobody can get them." Then come the deeds, with a distinction worth holding on to: a believer who has also taken full care of virtuous deeds receives the blessings of the Hereafter *right from the beginning*; one who has not may receive them only after being punished for his sins and shortcomings. But this is a general rule, not a cage around Allah: "if Allah Taʿālā wills, He may forgive all the sins of the greatest of the sinners, and give him the blessings of the Hereafter right from the beginning, He is not subject to any rule or code."

So the list that follows is a portrait of the believer who arrives without first passing through punishment.

## The seven traits

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān numbers them:

1. **They place their trust in their Lord** (36)
2. **They abstain from the major sins and from shameless acts** (37)
3. **When they get angry, they forgive** (37)
4. **They respond to their Lord and establish Salah** (38)
5. **Their affairs are settled by consultation between them** (38)
6. **They spend out of what We have given them** (38)
7. **When they are subjected to aggression, they defend themselves** (39)

**Trust (*tawakkul*).** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines it as placing trust in Allah "under all circumstances, in all matters," and adds the sharp edge: "they do not consider anyone else to be the real cause of anything." Ibn Kathir then ties trust back to the opening warning. He reads *"for those who believe"* as meaning "those who are patient in forgoing the pleasures of this world" — and *"and put their trust in their Lord"* as the reason they manage it: "so that He will help them to be patient in doing what is obligatory and avoiding what is forbidden." Trust here is not a feeling that everything will be fine. It is the strength supply that makes a restrained life possible.

**Abstaining from major sins and shameless acts** (ayah 37). Ibn Kathir notes that he has already discussed sin and *al-Fawāḥish* in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān refers the reader to its treatment of major sins in the commentary of Sūrah an-Nisāʼ. But Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers one question here: why single out shameless acts when they are already part of the major sins? Because "they are not only graver, but also infectious in that they influence others also." It specifies that shameless acts include adultery and the acts that precede it as preludes, and also "those bad deeds which are committed brazenly in public, because they corrupt the whole society and their liability is also very severe." A private sin injures the sinner; a flaunted sin lowers the floor for everyone.

## The trait the passage lingers on: anger and forgiveness

**"And when they are angry, they forgive"** (ayah 37). Ibn Kathir reads this as character rather than isolated incidents: "their nature dictates that they should forgive people and be tolerant. Vengeance is not in their nature."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why this is "a moral quality of the highest order." When love and anger prevail upon someone, "they make him blind and deaf, and he loses his ability to distinguish right from wrong, and true from false, rather, he cannot appreciate the results of his own actions." The one who is angry tries his utmost to vent his anger fully upon the one with whom he is angry. Against that, Allah describes believers who, in that exact state, "not only maintain the limits of right and wrong, but also forgo their justified rights" — they stay inside the boundary, and then give up something legitimately theirs.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir reports that it was reported in the Ṣaḥīḥ that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ never took revenge for his own sake, only when the sacred Laws of Allah were violated. The line is drawn precisely: personal injury, forgiven; violation of what Allah has made sacred, not a private matter to waive.

## Ayah 38: responding, praying, consulting, spending

**"Those who answer the Call of their Lord."** Ibn Kathir: "they follow His Messenger ﷺ and obey His commands and avoid that which He has prohibited." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the quality of the response — it means "to accept Allah's orders immediately, without questioning them, and get ready to obey them, irrespective of whether the order is or is not according to one's liking." That last clause is the test: obedience that only operates when the command suits us is not response, it is agreement.

**"And perform As-Salah."** Ibn Kathir calls it "the greatest act of worship of Allah, may He be glorified." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why Salah is named out of all the obligations that "responding to their Lord" already includes: it is "the most important of all the obligations," and it has "the quality of enabling discharge of other duties and avoidance of unlawful things." Prayer is not one item on the list; it is what drives the rest of the list.

**"And who (conduct) their affairs by mutual consultation" (*wa amruhum shūrā baynahum*).** Ibn Kathir: "they do not make a decision without consulting one another on the matter so that they can help one another by sharing their ideas concerning issues such as wars and other matters." He links it to *"and consult them in the affairs"* (3:159), and notes that the Prophet ﷺ used to consult with his Companions concerning wars and other matters, "so that they would feel confidant."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sharpens the scope in two directions. First, the *subject matter*: consultation is called for "in all important affairs where the Shariʿah is silent." It qualifies "affairs" with "important" because the word *amr* used in the text signifies importance in common usage; as clarified under 3:159, important affairs include affairs of the state as well as important affairs in general. Where Allah has ruled, there is nothing to put to consultation; where He has left room, deciding alone is the failure.

Second, the *weight*: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Ibn Kathir has stated that consultation in the important affairs of the state is compulsory. Imām Jaṣṣāṣ, in *Aḥkām al-Qurʼān*, is cited to the same effect — this verse "has made the importance of consultation evident, and we are under orders to consult wise and far sighted people for taking action in important matters requiring advice, and not to act hurriedly relying only on ourselves."

**A historical illustration.** Ibn Kathir gives a case in point. When ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him) was dying, after he had been stabbed, he entrusted the choice of the next Khalīfah to six people who were to be consulted: ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, Ṭalḥah, az-Zubayr, Saʿīd and ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf (may Allah be pleased with them all). Then all of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) agreed to appoint ʿUthmān as their leader.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the political point: the selection of the head of the state through consultation, ordained by Islam, "brought to an end the autocratic rule of kings of the days of ignorance who used to take the state as an inherited estate." But it does not simply baptise modern politics: Islam, "unlike western democracies, has not given total authority to the public," and there are certain restrictions on the members of the advisory body — the system of government in Islam "is a very moderate one, quite apart from autocracy and western democracy."

**Who gets consulted.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Khaṭīb Baghdādī (via *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*): Sayyidunā ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) asked the Prophet ﷺ how they should proceed if, after him, they faced a situation about which the Qurʼān had no specific ruling and he had given no direction. He ﷺ replied: "In such a case, assemble *ʿābidīn* (the worshipping people) of my ummah, and decide the matter by mutual consultation; do not take decision on any individual's single opinion." In some versions of this narration the word *fuqahāʼ* (jurists) also appears alongside the worshippers, which means that the jurists who have understanding of the religion and the worshippers are the ones who should be consulted. The author of *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī* warns that if this process is not followed — if irreligious people and people without proper knowledge of religion are consulted instead — "the ill effects would prevail upon the good in their advice."

So *shūrā* is not counting heads. It is asking the right heads.

**The promise attached to consultation.** Bayhaqī narrated in *Shuʿab al-Īmān* from Sayyidunā Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said, "Anyone who intends to do something, and he takes that action after consultation, Allah Taʿālā would guide him towards the best possible option" — meaning, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, that He will turn that person's direction towards an option that results in his betterment. A similar hadith reported by Sayyidunā Ḥasan (may Allah be pleased with him) is reproduced by Bukhārī in *al-Adab al-Mufrad* and by ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd in his *Musnad*: the Prophet ﷺ, after reciting this very verse, said, "When a nation takes an action after mutual consultation, it is surely guided towards the correct course."

**"And who spend of what We have bestowed on them."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes this as spending for virtuous deeds — zakāh, and obligatory and optional alms. Ibn Kathir reads it as "kindly treating the creation of Allah, starting with those who are closest, then the next closest, and so on" — kindness that moves outward in rings from the household.

**An observation on the ordering.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, quoting *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*, that the Qurʼān usually mentions zakāh and *ṣadaqāt* immediately after Salah; here consultation is mentioned in between, "perhaps to attract attention to the possibility of utilizing the five times daily salah congregation in mosques for the purpose of consultation also in matters which require mutual consultation." The prayer gathers the community; while it is gathered, let it decide.

## Ayah 39: and yet — when aggression strikes

Having praised those who forgive when angry, the passage now praises those who, "when they are subjected to aggression, defend themselves." Is that a contradiction?

**First, what the word means.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the original word *yantaṣirūn* "may be translated as 'defend themselves' and also as 'retaliate.'" In the latter case, "retaliation must be equal, and should in no case exceed the limit of equality."

**Second, what the trait praises.** Ibn Kathir's reading is subtle: the verse means "they have the strength to take revenge on those who commit aggressive wrong and hostile acts against them. They are not incapable of doing so and they are not helpless." What is being praised is *capacity* — so that their forgiveness in ayah 37 is not the forgiveness of the weak, who could not have retaliated anyway. As he puts it, "even though when they have the power to take revenge, they prefer to forgive."

Ibn Kathir gives three illustrations. Yūsuf (peace be upon him), though he was in a position to take revenge on his brothers for what they had done to him, said instead: *"No reproach on you this day; may Allah forgive you"* (12:92). The Messenger of Allah ﷺ forgave the eighty people who intended to do him harm during the year of al-Ḥudaybiyah, camping by the mountain of at-Tanʿīm — when he overpowered them he set them free, even though he was in a position to take revenge on them. And he ﷺ forgave Ghawrath ibn al-Ḥārith, who wanted to kill him and unsheathed his sword while he was sleeping; the Prophet ﷺ woke to find him pointing the sword at him, reproached him angrily, and the sword dropped. He ﷺ then picked up the sword, called his Companions, told them what had happened — and forgave the man. Ibn Kathir adds that there are many similar hadiths and reports, "and Allah knows best."

**Third, when redress is the better choice.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this quality "in reality, is a further elaboration of the third virtue, i.e. forgiving the opponents" rather than cancelling it: forgiveness is a good quality, "yet one may face certain situations where the mischief gets a fillip if one forgives" — where pardon simply funds more wrongdoing — "and hence it is better to take revenge in those situations." Even then the limit binds: in situations where redress is the more suitable option, "one has to take care that one does not exceed the equalizing limit, otherwise he will become unjust and transgressor."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this is why the following verse lays down the equitable rule of retaliation — that one may cause just as much physical or monetary harm to his opponent as he has received from him, on the condition that causing that harm is not a sin in itself. Its illustration: if someone has been forced by another to take an alcoholic drink, it would not be permissible for him to force the other person to take an alcoholic drink. And although permission is given to take redress in equal measure, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the emphasis immediately returns to pardon — "the one who forgives and compromises has his reward undertaken by Allah" — so that "the instruction is that to forgive is better."

**How the scholars settled it.** Ibrāhīm Nakhaʿī (may Allah have mercy on him) stated that the former virtuous elders did not like that Muslims be disgraced and debased by the sinners and oppressors who, if not taken to task, may be encouraged to further wrongdoing. So where it is feared that the sinners and oppressors would become more daring and would harass decent people if they are forgiven, it is better to take redress from them; and forgiveness is better where the transgressor is repentant and there is no apprehension of his becoming more daring. Qāḍī Abū Bakr Ibn al-ʿArabī in *Aḥkām al-Qurʼān* and Qurṭubī in his *Tafsīr* concurred: forgiveness and redress are applicable as suitable, in different situations — for one who is repentant after having transgressed it is better to forgive, and for one who is stubborn and insistent upon transgression it is better to take redress.

Maulānā Ashraf ʿAlī Thānawī (may Allah have mercy on him) explained the issue in *Bayān al-Qurʼān* from a slightly different angle: in both verses Allah has mentioned two qualities particular to the true, sincere and virtuous Muslims. The verse emphasising forgiveness tells us they are not overcome by anger — kindness and generosity remain dominant in their temperament, because of which they forgive those who commit excess against them. And the verse referring to redress tells us that if at any time their heart is inclined to answer an injustice and they do so, they do not exceed the equitable limit, "although to forgive is always better for them."

## Living it

**Re-price what you hold.** Ayah 36 does not tell you to own nothing. It tells you not to be deceived by what you own, because you know the terms: transient here, lasting there. The test is what you will trade for what.

**Take your anger seriously as worship.** The moment of anger is where ayah 37 is won or lost. The believer's mark, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes it, is not the absence of anger; it is that inside the anger he keeps the limits of right and wrong, and then forgoes a right that was genuinely his.

**Do not decide alone.** Where the Shariʿah has spoken, follow. Where it is silent and the matter is important — family, community, work, the affairs of a people — consult, and consult people of religion and understanding. The Prophet ﷺ, who received revelation, still consulted his Companions. Anyone who thinks he needs it less has misread himself.

passages.title: Justice, pardon, and the limits of retaliation
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat set out how a believer is to answer being wronged. Ayah 40 fixes the outer limit of any response — repayment may not exceed the injury — and in the same breath opens a better door: pardon and reconciliation, with the reward left with Allah. Ayat 41 and 42 then clear the wronged person of blame and place the burden of sin on the one who began, and ayah 43 closes the passage by placing patient forgiveness among the things recommended by Allah.

What holds them together is a single moral architecture: **justice sets the ceiling, forgiveness is the better way, and the burden of sin rests on whoever started it.**

## Ayah 40: "the recompense of an evil is an evil like it"

**وَجَزَٰٓؤُاْ سَيِّئَةٖ سَيِّئَةٞ مِّثۡلُهَا** — *The recompense for an evil is an evil like thereof.*

The decisive word is **mithluhā**, "the like of it." Not more. The like of it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes where this rule falls in the flow of the surah. The seventh of the believers' qualities listed there is in ayah 39: *"and those who, when they are subjected to aggression, defend themselves."* The word used is **yantaṣirūn**, which Maʿārif says may be translated both as "defend themselves" and as "retaliate" — and in the latter case, Maʿārif adds, retaliation must be equal and should in no case exceed the limit of equality. That, Maʿārif explains, is precisely why ayah 40 follows: it lays down the equitable rule of retaliation, so that one who takes the more suitable option of redress does not exceed the equalising limit and thereby become unjust and a transgressor himself.

Ibn Kathir places this alongside two sister ayat that say the same thing in other words:

- *"Then whoever transgresses the prohibition against you, you transgress likewise against him"* (2:194)
- *"And if you punish, then punish them with the like of that with which you were afflicted"* (16:126)

His summary of the whole matter is worth memorising: **justice has been prescribed** — in the form of the prescribed laws of equality in punishment, *al-Qiṣāṣ* — **but the better way, which means forgiving, is recommended.** He then quotes the ayah that holds both together in a single line: *"and wounds equal for equal. But if anyone remits the retaliation by way of charity, it shall be for him an expiation"* (5:45).

**The practical rule.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what "like it" means in practice: one may cause his opponent just as much physical or monetary harm as he received from him — with one crucial condition, that **causing that harm must not be a sin in itself.** Their example is sharply memorable: if someone has been forced by another to take an alcoholic drink, it is not permissible for him to force that person to take an alcoholic drink in return. The scale of redress is capped by the injury *and* by the sacred law at the same time.

## "But whoever pardons and makes reconciliation"

**فَمَنۡ عَفَا وَأَصۡلَحَ فَأَجۡرُهُۥ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ** — *But whoever forgives and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah.*

Two verbs, not one. **ʿAfā** — to pardon. **Aṣlaḥa** — to make reconciliation, to set right what was broken.

Maʿārif observes the movement here: permission has been given in this ayah to take redress in equal measure, and immediately thereafter it is emphasised again that the one who forgives and compromises has his reward *undertaken by Allah*. The instruction, Maʿārif says plainly, is that **to forgive is better.**

Ibn Kathir's comment on *"his reward is with Allah"* is simply: **it will not be wasted with Allah.** He supports this with what he identifies as a Sahih Hadith, without naming a collection for it: **"Allah does not increase the person who forgives except in honour."**

## "Verily, He likes not the wrongdoers"

The ayah closes with **إِنَّهُۥ لَا يُحِبُّ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ**.

Ibn Kathir specifies who is meant: **the aggressors — those who initiate the evil actions.** The ayah has just permitted a measured response; the gloss makes clear that what stands condemned is the *starting* of injustice.

## Ayat 41–42: where the blame actually lands

**وَلَمَنِ ٱنتَصَرَ بَعۡدَ ظُلۡمِهِۦ فَأُوْلَٰٓئِكَ مَا عَلَيۡهِم مِّن سَبِيلٖ** — *And indeed whosoever takes revenge after he has suffered wrong, for such there is no way (of blame) against them.*

Ibn Kathir: **there is no sin on him for taking revenge against the one who wronged him.** Forgiveness is the better way — but standing up for a right that was taken is not itself a fault.

Ayah 42 then identifies who *does* carry the weight. Ibn Kathir explains the key word **al-sabīl** — literally "the way," here meaning **the burden of sin**. So the sense is: the burden of sin lies only upon *"those who oppress men and rebel in the earth without justification"* — which, in Ibn Kathir's words, means **those who initiate wrongful actions against others.**

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites here what he identifies as a Sahih Hadith, again without naming a collection:

> "When two persons indulge in abusing each other, the one who initiated the wrongful action is to blame, unless the one who was wronged oversteps the mark in retaliation."

This is the passage compressed into a sentence. In an exchange of insults, the blame sits on the one who began — *unless* the wronged party oversteps in retaliation. That exception is exactly why ayah 40 insisted on *mithluhā* before anything else was said.

Of *"for such there will be a painful torment,"* Ibn Kathir says simply: **intense and agonising.**

## A story the sources tell: what it takes to be free of blame

Ibn Kathir reports an account (recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim) of how ayah 42 was invoked before a man in power.

Muhammad bin Wasiʿ said that he came to Makkah, and the guards of a security post over the trench took him to Marwan bin al-Muhallab, the governor of Basrah. The governor asked him, "What do you need, O Abu ʿAbdullah?" He answered: "If you can do it, I need you to be like the brother of Banu ʿAdiy." Asked who that was, he named **al-ʿAlāʾ bin Ziyad**, who had once appointed a friend of his to a position of authority and written to him:

> If you can, only go to sleep after you make sure that there is nothing on your back [i.e., you do not owe anything to anyone], your stomach is empty, and your hands are untainted by the blood or wealth of the Muslims. If you do that, then there will be no way (of blame) against you —

and he then recited ayah 42: *"The way is only against those who oppress men and rebel in the earth without justification; for such there will be a painful torment."*

Marwan said, "He spoke the truth, by Allah, and gave sincere advice." Then he asked again what Muhammad bin Wasiʿ needed, and he said, "I need you to let me join my family." The governor granted it.

Read the letter's three conditions again: nothing owed, the stomach empty, the hands untainted by the blood or wealth of the Muslims. Whoever can lie down on that, the letter says, has no *sabīl* against him.

## Ayah 43: patience, concealment, and the things recommended by Allah

**وَلَمَن صَبَرَ وَغَفَرَ إِنَّ ذَٰلِكَ لَمِنۡ عَزۡمِ ٱلۡأُمُورِ**

Ibn Kathir marks the order of the passage: **when Allah condemned wrongdoing and the people who do it, and prescribed al-Qiṣāṣ, He encouraged forgiveness.**

He then unpacks the two verbs of ayah 43 concretely. *Ṣabara* — **to bear the insult with patience.** *Ghafara* — **to conceal the evil action.** That second gloss is worth sitting with: on Ibn Kathir's reading, what the ayah praises includes not exposing what was done to you.

**ʿAzm al-umūr.** The phrase is rendered here as *"the things recommended by Allah,"* and Ibn Kathir transmits from **Saʿīd bin Jubayr**: "This means, one of the things enjoined by Allah" — that is, **good actions for which there will be a great reward and much praise.**

## When to pardon and when to respond: the scholars weigh in

The practical question this passage raises is which door to walk through. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers the answers under the heading *"The Moderate decision between forgiveness and revenge."*

**Ibrahim Nakhaʿī** (may Allah have mercy on him) stated that the virtuous elders of the past did not like that Muslims should be disgraced and debased by sinners and oppressors who, if not taken to task, may be encouraged to further wrongdoing. Therefore: **where it is apprehended that the sinners and oppressors would become more daring and would harass decent people if forgiven, it is better to take redress from them.** And **to forgive would be better where the transgressor is repentant and there is no apprehension of his becoming more daring.**

**Qadi Abu Bakr Ibn al-ʿArabi** in *Aḥkām ul-Qurʼān* and **al-Qurtubi** in his *Tafsir* concurred with this view: forgiveness and redress are applicable as suited to different situations — for one who is repentant after having transgressed it is better to forgive, and for one who is stubborn and insistent upon transgression it is better to take redress.

**Maulana Ashraf ʿAli Thanawi** (may Allah have mercy on him), in *Bayān ul-Qurʼān*, explains the issue — as Maʿārif puts it — "from a little different angle." He says that Allah has mentioned in both ayat two qualities particular to the true, sincere and virtuous Muslims. The ayah emphasising forgiveness tells us **they are not overcome by anger**; rather kindness and generosity remain dominant in their temperament, which is why they forgive those who commit excess against them. And the ayah referring to redress tells us it is a particular quality of these virtuous people that **if at some time their heart is inclined to answer an injustice and they do so, they do not exceed the equitable limit** — although to forgive is always better for them.

## Living it

- **Fix the ceiling before you act.** The first thing ayah 40 hands you is a limit: *mithluhā*, the like of it, and no more. Maʿārif warns that exceeding the equalising limit makes the one who exceeds it unjust and a transgressor.
- **Never let redress become a sin.** Maʿārif's condition is explicit: causing the harm must not be a sin in itself.
- **Ask which case you are in.** Is this person repentant, or would leniency embolden him to harass others? The scholars Maʿārif cites make that the deciding question.
- **When you pardon, pardon fully.** ʿAfā *and* aṣlaḥa; ṣabara *and* ghafara — pardon and make reconciliation; bear the insult patiently and conceal the evil action.
- **Trust the reward left with Allah.** *"His reward is with Allah"* — Ibn Kathir says it will not be wasted with Allah, and that the one who forgives is increased by Allah in nothing but honour.
- **Check your own hands.** Al-ʿAlāʾ bin Ziyad's letter is a nightly audit: nothing owed, the stomach empty, the hands untainted by the blood or wealth of the Muslims.

passages.title: The misguided at the Fire, and the summons before the Day
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat take you to the edge of the Fire, let you watch the faces of those standing there, and then turn round and speak to you — while there is still time. The unity of the passage is a single question asked twice, in two opposite directions. In ayah 44 the wrongdoers ask, at the Fire, *"Is there any way of return?"* — and the answer is no. In ayah 47 we are called to answer our Lord now, before a Day comes *"which cannot be averted"*. The scene is painted so that the summons will land.

## "No protector after Him" (ayah 44)

The passage opens with a statement about Allah's absolute will. Ibn Kathir sets it out plainly: whatever Allah wills happens, and whatever He does not will does not happen, and no one can make it happen; whomever He guides, none can lead astray, and whomever He leads astray, none can guide. He brings the parallel from Sūrat al-Kahf: *"but he whom He sends astray, for him you will find no protecting to lead him"* (18:17).

So the ayah's own words stand: *"whomsoever Allah sends astray, for him there is no protector after Him."* This is the ground of everything else in the passage — and it is also why ayah 47 will read as a mercy rather than a threat, because the One who alone can guide is the One who is calling.

Ibn Kathir identifies the "wrongdoers" here specifically as the idolaters — those who associate others in worship with Allah.

## The scene at the Fire (ayat 44–45)

**"Is there any way of return?"** They see the punishment, and what breaks out of them is not repentance but a wish to be sent back to the world — Ibn Kathir says exactly that: on the Day of Resurrection they will wish that they could go back to this world. He pairs the moment with al-Anʿām:

> *"If you could but see when they will be held over the (Hell) Fire! They will say: 'Would that we were but sent back! Then we would not deny the Ayat of our Lord, and we would be of the believers!'
