Nay, it has become manifest to them what they had been concealing before. But if they were returned, they would certainly revert to that which they were forbidden. And indeed they are liars."* (6:27–28)

That is a devastating gloss. The wish is real as a wish, but it is not a change of heart. Returned to the world, they would return to exactly what they were.

**Watch how they are brought.** In ayah 45 they are *"brought forward to it"* — Ibn Kathir notes simply: to the Fire. The wording puts them on the receiving end; they are brought, they do not come.

Then two phrases give you their bodies and their eyes:

- ***khāshiʿīna mina l-dhull*** — "made humble by disgrace." Ibn Kathir comments that this is in a befitting manner, because of their previous disobedience towards Allah. The abasement matches what they did.
- ***yanẓurūna min ṭarfin khafiyy*** — "looking with stealthy glance." Mujahid explained it as "in a humiliated manner." Ibn Kathir draws out the psychology: they will steal glances at it because they will be afraid of it — but the thing they are afraid of will undoubtedly happen, and worse than that. He breaks off the commentary to pray: may Allah save us from that.

Anyone who has watched a person unable to look directly at what is coming for them knows this sideways glance. The Qur'an renders terror in a single movement of the eye.

## The believers' verdict (ayah 45)

At that moment the believers speak. Ibn Kathir places their words on the Day of Resurrection itself: *"Verily, the losers are they who lose themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection."*

*Al-khāsirīn* — the losers. Ibn Kathir glosses it as **the greatest losers**. And he specifies the double loss: they will be taken to the Fire and deprived of any pleasures in the Hereafter — that is losing *themselves*; and they will be separated from their loved ones, companions, families and relatives — that is losing their *families*.

This is worth sitting with. Every worldly loss leaves you something: lose money, you still have your people; lose your people, you still have yourself. Here, on Ibn Kathir's reading, both columns are emptied at once — the self and the family, the two accounts people actually keep, written off together.

Then the seal: ***alā inna l-ẓālimīna fī ʿadhābin muqīm*** — "the wrongdoers will be in a lasting torment." Ibn Kathir: everlasting and eternal, with no way out and no escape.

## Two doors closed (ayah 46)

Ayah 46 closes the two doors a person might still hope for.

First, help from outside: *"And they will have no protectors to help them other than Allah"* — Ibn Kathir: no one to save them from the punishment and torment which they are suffering. In this world the wrongdoer has patrons, allies, a network. There it is empty.

Second, escape from within: *"And he whom Allah sends astray, for him there is no way"* — *fa-mā lahu min sabīl* — Ibn Kathir: **no salvation**.

Notice also how the wording answers their own question. They asked, *hal ilā maraddin min sabīl* — "Is there any way of return?" Ayah 46 ends with the same word they used: *min sabīl* — there is no way.

## The summons: respond before the Day (ayah 47)

Having shown the horror, Allah now commands preparation for it. Ibn Kathir heads this section *Encouragement to obey Allah before the Day of Resurrection*, and explains: when Allah tells us about the horrors and terrifying events of the Day of Resurrection, He warns us about it and commands us to prepare for it.

***Istajībū li-rabbikum*** — "Answer the Call of your Lord." The command is not merely to believe in your Lord but to answer Him — which is what faith looks like when it moves. And the One being answered is named as *Rabb*, your Lord: the call comes from the One who has the right to call.

*"before there comes from Allah a Day which cannot be averted"* (*lā maradda lahu*). Ibn Kathir: once He issues the command, it will come to pass within the blinking of an eye, and no one will be able to avert it or prevent it. And here is the passage's sharpest hinge — *maradd* is the same word the wrongdoers used at the Fire when they asked for a *maradd*, a return. They wanted a return that does not exist; the Day itself admits no turning back. The only return available is the one offered right now, in this ayah.

Then two refusals for that Day:

- ***mā lakum min malja'*** — "you will have no refuge." Ibn Kathir: you will have no stronghold in which to take refuge, no place in which to hide from Allah, for He will encompass you with His knowledge and power. Then he adds a line that turns the whole verse from terror to invitation: **you will have no refuge from Him except with Him.**
- ***wa mā lakum min nakīr*** — "nor there will be for you any denying." The option of denial is gone.

Ibn Kathir brings al-Qiyāmah alongside: *"On that Day man will say: 'Where (is the refuge) to flee?' No! There is no refuge! Unto your Lord will be the place of rest that Day."* (75:10–12)

Maarif ul Quran reads ayah 47 in exactly this register: the earlier verses state the end of those who remained desirous of the delights and luxuries of this world instead of caring about the Hereafter, and then in verse 47 they are advised to repent and embrace faith before the scourge of Doomsday comes upon them. The whole grim panorama exists to make a call to repentance credible.

## Comfort for the Prophet ﷺ (ayah 48)

*"But if they turn away, We have not sent you as a **Hafiz** over them. Your duty is to convey."*

Maarif ul Quran reads this as consolation: the Holy Prophet ﷺ is comforted and assured that if these people do not come to their senses, despite his preaching again and again and despite his tireless efforts, he should not worry — *"We did not send you as a supervisor over them. You are not responsible but for conveying the message."*

Ibn Kathir's gloss on *Hafiz* is short and complete: *you have no power over them.* (He notes that "if they turn away" refers to the idolaters.) He supports it with two other ayat:

- *"Not upon you is their guidance, but Allah guides whom He wills"* (2:272)
- *"your duty is only to convey (the Message) and on Us is the reckoning"* (13:40)

And of *in ʿalayka illā l-balāgh* — "Your duty is to convey" — Ibn Kathir writes: all that We require you to do is to convey the Message of Allah to them.

**Living it.** This is the passage's most immediately practical line for anyone who carries concern for someone else's faith — a child, a parent, a friend. The instruction, at its highest expression in the Prophet ﷺ himself, is: your responsibility is the *balāgh*, the conveying. The result is not your department. Ayah 44 already told you why — Allah guides whom He wills, and whomever He leaves to stray has no protector after Him. To take the outcome onto your own shoulders is to claim a role that Allah did not give even to His Messenger ﷺ. That frees you both from despair when someone refuses, and from the temptation to force what only Allah can give.

## Man's ingratitude (ayah 48)

The passage closes by describing how people receive what comes to them: *"And verily, when We cause man to taste of mercy from Us, he rejoices thereat; but when some evil befalls them because of the deeds which their hands have sent forth, then verily, man (becomes) ingrate."*

Ibn Kathir unpacks each piece. The mercy is a time of ease and comfort coming to him, and he is happy about it. The "evil" is drought, punishment, tribulation or difficulty. And of *kafūr*, "ingrate," he writes with real psychological precision:

> he forgets the previous times of ease and blessings and acknowledges nothing but the present moment. If times of ease come to him, he becomes arrogant and transgresses, but if any difficulty befalls him, he loses hope and is filled with despair.

That is the flaw: a memory only one day long. Blessings received for years are erased by one hard week. Note too that the verse says the evil comes *because of the deeds which their hands have sent forth*.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir illustrates this with what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to the women — the bundle does not name the collection, so it is given here simply as Ibn Kathir reports it. He ﷺ said: *"O women, give in charity, for I have seen that you form the majority of the people of Hell."* A woman asked, "Why is that, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: *"Because you complain too much, and you are ungrateful to (your) husbands. If one of you were to be treated kindly for an entire lifetime, then that kindness was lacking for one day, she would say, 'I have never seen anything good from you!'"* Ibn Kathir immediately qualifies it: this is the case with most women, except for those whom Allah guides and who are among the people who believe and do righteous deeds. And in this context the report functions as a mirror for the *kafūr* the ayah names — one bad day cancelling a lifetime of good is precisely the forgetfulness Ibn Kathir has just described.

Against it, Ibn Kathir sets the Prophet's ﷺ description of the believer: *"...if something good happens to him, he is thankful, and that is good for him. If something bad happens to him, he bears it with patience, and that is good for him. This does not happen to anyone except the believer."*

That is the answer to the whole passage. Ayah 48 shows two ways of receiving your life. The ungrateful way ends at the scene in ayat 44–46 — the sideways glance, the request for a return that is not granted. The believer's way, thankful in ease and patient in hardship, is what *"Answer the Call of your Lord"* in ayah 47 looks like when it is lived out on an ordinary day.

passages.title: Daughters, sons, and the will behind every birth
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat take the argument of the sūrah down from the vastness of the heavens and the earth to the most intimate thing in a human life — who is in the cradle, and whether there is a cradle at all. Ayah 49 declares that the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah and that He creates whatever He wills; ayah 50 completes the sentence by naming four kinds of household, and closes with two names: **al-ʿAlīm**, the All-Knower, and **al-Qadīr**, the One Able to do all things. What holds the passage together is a single move: the proof of Allah's absolute sovereignty is placed not in the stars but in the family, where every human being has felt the limits of his own will.

## Where this comes in the sūrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the thread. The verses just before this described people who remained desirous of the delights and luxuries of this world instead of caring about the Hereafter; in ayah 47 they were advised to repent and embrace faith before the scourge of Doomsday comes upon them. Then in ayah 48 the Prophet ﷺ himself was comforted and assured that if these people do not come to their senses despite his tireless efforts, he should not worry: *"So, if they turn away, then We did not send you as a supervisor over them. You are not responsible but for conveying the message."*

That is exactly why ayat 49–50 come next. Having told His Messenger ﷺ that he is not the one who controls outcomes, Allah now states who does. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says these two verses state **the absolute power and perfect wisdom of Allah in the creation of this universe, in which He has no partner**, and on that basis mankind is called to believe in His Oneness. The consolation and the argument are the same truth seen from two sides: the results are not in your hands, because they were never in anyone's hands but His.

## Ayah 49: ownership before action

The ayah opens by establishing ownership — *"To Allah belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth"* — before it mentions any act. Ibn Kathir draws out three things at once from this: Allah is **the Creator, Sovereign and Controller** of the heavens and the earth.

Then comes the rule that governs everything after it, in Ibn Kathir's words:

> Whatever He wills happens, and whatever He does not will does not happen. He gives to whomsoever He wills and withholds from whomsoever He wills; none can withhold what He gives, and none can give what He withholds, and He creates whatever He wills.

Notice the shape of that sentence: giving and withholding are placed on the same shelf. Both are acts of the same Owner, and neither can be reversed by anyone else.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lingers on the phrase *yakhluqu mā yashāʾ*, **"He creates what He wills."** The point of the words, it says, is to indicate that He has absolute power to create anything small or big — He creates whatever He wills, whenever He wills. The sentence is deliberately unbounded so that nothing can be imagined outside it.

**A giving, not a producing.** The passage does not speak of children being produced or arranged. Ibn Kathir's rendering is **"He bestows"**; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's is **"He grants."** Both words describe something handed over by a giver. Children, on the reading of these commentators, come as something granted by the One who owns the heavens and the earth — and the same ayah that names the granting also names the withholding.

## The four households

Ibn Kathir reads ayat 49–50 as sorting all people into four categories, and Al-Baghawī, whom Ibn Kathir quotes here, gives a prophet as the living example of each:

**1. Daughters only.** *"He bestows female upon whom He wills"* — Ibn Kathir: He gives them daughters only. Al-Baghawī said, "And among them was **Lūṭ**, peace be upon him."

**2. Sons only.** *"And bestows male upon whom He wills"* — He gives them sons only. Al-Baghawī said, "Like **Ibrāhīm al-Khalīl**, peace be upon him, who did not have any daughters."

**3. Both together.** *"Or He bestows both males and females"* — Ibn Kathir: He gives to whomsoever He wills both males and females, sons and daughters. Al-Baghawī said: **"Like Muhammad ﷺ."**

**4. No children at all.** *"And He renders barren whom He wills"* — Ibn Kathir explains this as *so that he has no children at all*. Al-Baghawī said, "Like **Yaḥyā and ʿĪsā**, peace be upon them." (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān phrases this category as Allah rendering some women barren, so that they do not have any children.)

Ibn Kathir then states the division plainly: **some are given daughters, some are given sons, some are given both sons and daughters, and some are not given either, but are rendered barren, with no offspring.**

Sit with that list for a moment, because it is doing pastoral work, not just theological work. Every one of the four situations a family can find itself in — including the two that people quietly grieve over, a house with no sons and a house with no children — is illustrated in this commentary by a prophet of Allah. A household of daughters only was the household of Lūṭ, peace be upon him. Yaḥyā and ʿĪsā, peace be upon them, are named in the category with no offspring. These categories are not accidents that fell outside the plan; they are distributions from the One who owns everything.

## "He knows" and "He is Able"

The two closing names in ayah 50 are not decoration; Ibn Kathir gives each a precise job in the argument.

**إِنَّهُ عَلِيمٌ — "Verily, He is the All-Knower."** Ibn Kathir: this means **He knows who deserves to be in which of these categories**. So the four-way distribution is not a lottery. It is allotment by perfect knowledge of what each person deserves — knowledge that the person himself does not have about his own life.

**قَدِيرٌ — "and is Able to do all things."** Ibn Kathir: able to do whatever He wills, and **to differentiate between people in this manner**. The very unevenness of human families — why this house and not that one — is itself presented as evidence of power.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the same point from the human side, and the force of it is worth keeping: **nobody's intention or authority has anything to do with the creation of a human being, nor does anybody have its knowledge.** Even the intention or choice of the parents, who are the apparent agents of a child's creation, does not have any bearing on it. And it goes further: the mother does not even know, before the child is born, what is being formed in her womb, or how it is being processed. The two closing names answer exactly those two gaps — the knowledge that is not ours (*ʿAlīm*), and the power that is not ours (*Qadīr*).

## Daughters named first

There is a detail in the wording that the commentators did not pass over. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that while stating the sex of children in this verse, **Allah has mentioned females first, and males later** — He grants females to whom He wills, and then males to whom He wills.

And it reports, on the authority of Qurṭubī, that taking a hint from this verse **Sayyidnā Wāthilah ibn al-Asqaʿ (may Allah be pleased with him) said that blessed is the woman who gives birth to a daughter first.** A blessing was drawn straight out of the order of the words.

Even the third category is expressed with a word of pairing: *aw yuzawwijuhum dhukrānan wa-ināthā*, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders as **"He combines for them couples, both males and females"** — sons and daughters set side by side in one household.

## The second set of four: how parents themselves came to be

Ibn Kathir then lifts the argument one level higher, and this is among the most striking parts of his commentary here. He connects it to what Allah says of ʿĪsā, peace be upon him: **"And We wish to appoint him as a sign to mankind"** (19:21) — meaning, he says, **proof for them of His power**. For Allah created people in four different ways:

- **Ādam**, peace be upon him, created from clay — **from neither a male nor a female**.
- **Ḥawwāʾ**, peace be upon her, created **from a male without a female**.
- **All other people**, besides ʿĪsā, peace be upon him — created **from male and female**.
- **ʿĪsā ibn Maryam**, may peace be upon them both — created **from a female without a male**, and with him, Ibn Kathir says, this sign of Allah was completed.

Then he sets the two lists beside each other: **this issue has to do with parents, whilst the previous issue has to do with children, and in each case there are four categories.** The symmetry is the argument. Every way a human being can be brought into existence, and every way a household can be given, is accounted for — leaving no version of the human story that stands outside His will. Ibn Kathir ends the passage with the only fitting response: *Glory be to the All-Knower Who is Able to do all things.*

## Living it

**Stop assigning blame for what was never a human decision.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is blunt: the intention or choice of the parents, the apparent agents of a child's creation, has no bearing on it — and the mother does not even know what is being formed in her womb. The passage removes any ground for reproaching a wife over the sex of a child, or a couple over having no child. That is a matter settled in the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, not in a marriage.

**Receive daughters as the ayah presents them** — named first, and named as something granted. A household of daughters only is, in Al-Baghawī's example, the household of Lūṭ, peace be upon him; a household of both is, in his example, that of Muhammad ﷺ; and Wāthilah ibn al-Asqaʿ (may Allah be pleased with him) called the woman blessed whose first child is a daughter.

**Read your own family as evidence, not verdict.** Whichever of the four categories you are in, ayah 50 says the One who placed you there is *ʿAlīm* — He knows who deserves to be in which — and *Qadīr* — able to do whatever He wills, since none can withhold what He gives and none can give what He withholds.

**And take the consolation that ayah 48 was offering the Prophet ﷺ.** If the outcome of the most personal effort a person makes — building a family — was never in his hands, then the outcome of his preaching, his work, and his hopes for others is not in his hands either. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, he is not responsible but for conveying the message. Convey, strive, and leave the result with the Owner of the heavens and the earth.

passages.title: The three ways Allah speaks, and the Path He guides to
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat close Surah ash-Shura by answering one question: how does Allah actually speak to a human being? Ayah 51 lays out the only three ways it happens; ayah 52 applies that to the Prophet ﷺ and to the Qur'an he received; ayah 53 names where the road he calls people to leads — to Allah, the Lord and Sovereign of the heavens and the earth, to Whom all matters at the end go. What holds the passage together is a single movement: from the manner of revelation, to the content of revelation, to the destination revelation points toward.

## The challenge that prompted the ayah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports — citing Baghawi, Qurtubi and others — that ayah 51 was revealed in response to a hostile Jewish demand. They asked the Prophet ﷺ: *"How can we believe in you while you neither see Allah Taʿala, nor do you speak to Him face to face, as Sayyidna Musa (peace be upon him) used to see and converse with Allah Taʿala?"*

It was a challenge dressed as a theological objection. The Prophet ﷺ first corrected the premise itself: he told them that it is wrong to say that Musa (peace be upon him) had seen Allah. Then this ayah was revealed to announce the matter at its root — **it is not possible for any human being to converse with Allah face to face in this world.** Musa (peace be upon him) did not hear Allah face to face either; he heard the voice from behind a curtain.

So the objection collapses. The objectors were measuring Muhammad ﷺ against a standard that had never existed for anyone, Musa included. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls their demand plainly "a display of ignorance and hostility." And the ayah does not merely refute them — it turns the refutation into positive teaching: here is how Allah *does* speak.

## The three ways

Ayah 51 gives an exclusive list — "It is not given to any human being that Allah should speak to him **unless**…" — and then three exceptions.

**1. By waḥy — something cast into the heart.** Ibn Kathir explains that sometimes Allah casts something into the heart of the Prophet ﷺ, and he has no doubt that it is from Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes this as "infusion of something in the heart," which can happen while a person is awake, and can also happen during sleep in the form of a dream. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that it is stated in many ahadith that the Prophet ﷺ said *ulqiya fī rūʿī* — "This has been infused in my heart."

The dreams of the prophets belong here too, and are a form of waḥy, because Shaytan cannot find his way into them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a careful detail: in the case of dreams the words do not usually come from Allah — only the subject matter is infused in the mind, which the prophets then render in their own words.

Ibn Kathir cites here a hadith reported in **Sahih Ibn Hibban**, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Ar-Ruh Al-Qudus [i.e., Jibril] breathed into my heart that no soul will die until its allotted provision and time have expired, so have Taqwa of Allah and keep seeking in a good (and lawful) way."

Notice how the mode and the message match. A truth breathed quietly into the heart is a truth about the quiet arithmetic of your life: your provision is measured out, your term is fixed, and neither will be cut short. And the practical conclusion drawn in the hadith itself is not "stop working" — it is to *keep seeking in a good and lawful way*. Since no anxious scramble will win you anything beyond what has been allotted, pursue your livelihood with taqwā and by lawful means.

**2. From behind a veil.** Ibn Kathir glosses "or from behind a veil" simply: "as He spoke to Musa, peace be upon him." He adds what followed — Musa "asked to see Him after He had spoken to him, but this was not granted to him." Ibn Kathir stops there, without naming a place or a verse.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in both. It places this second mode of address on **Mount Tur**, where Musa (peace be upon him) heard the speech of Allah but did not see Him; he therefore asked Allah to show Himself, and — in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words — "The reply was in negative, as mentioned by the Holy Qur'an in surah Aʿraf (7:143)."

Ibn Kathir also cites a hadith recorded **in the Sahih**, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Jabir bin ʿAbdullah (may Allah be pleased with him):

> "Allah never speaks to anyone except from behind a veil, but He spoke to your father directly."

Jabir's father was killed on the day of Uhud. Ibn Kathir resolves the apparent tension precisely: that direct address refers to the realm of **al-Barzakh**, whereas the ayah speaks of this earthly realm. The rule of ayah 51 is a rule for this world; it does not govern what Allah grants after death.

**3. That He sends a messenger.** The third way is that Allah sends a messenger who reveals what He wills by His leave. Ibn Kathir: "as Jibril, peace be upon him, and other angels came down to the Prophets, peace be upon them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the messenger could be Jibril or any other angel who carries Allah's message and reads it out to the prophet, and that this has been the most common way — **the whole of the Glorious Qur'an has been revealed in this fashion, through angels.** There are two forms in which the angel carries the message: sometimes he appears in his original form, and sometimes in human form.

A useful terminological note from Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: the word *waḥy* in the first of the three categories means infusion in the mind or heart only — but the word is often used for all kinds of divine discourse as well. In a lengthy hadith of **Bukhari**, a message sent through an angel is itself termed one kind of waḥy.

## What the "veil" actually is

This is the most beautiful point in the passage, and it is worth reading slowly.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān insists that the curtain which prevents man from seeing Allah **is not something which can hide Allah**, because nothing can hide His All-Pervasive Light. Rather, *it is the weakness of man's vision that becomes a curtain against seeing Allah.* The deficiency is on our side, not His.

Which is why the veil is not permanent. That is why, when his vision is strengthened in Paradise, every dweller of Heaven will be favoured with the ability to see Allah — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states this explicitly as **the creed of Ahl us-Sunnah wal-Jamaʿah**, in accordance with the explanations of the correct ahadith. The believer's longing to see his Lord is not a hope that will be disappointed; it is a hope deferred until the sight has been strengthened to bear it.

Two further clarifications from the same commentary:

- The rule is about **this world**. If the face-to-face conversation of the Prophet ﷺ with Allah during the Night of Ascension (Laylat al-Miʿrāj) is proved, as certain learned persons have stated, it would not negate this rule — because that conversation did not take place in this world, but in the heavens. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān leaves the matter with *Allah knows best*, and so should we; this is a place where the learned have differed and certainty is not ours to manufacture.
- The specific mention of **"a human being"** in this ayah is because the intention here is to address mankind. Otherwise, apparently Allah does not speak face to face even with the angels — as stated by Jibril (peace be upon him) in a narration of **Tirmidhi**: *"I had become very close, and yet there were seventy-thousand more curtains."* Jibril, at the summit of nearness, still with seventy thousand curtains before him. Set that beside the demand that Allah should simply speak to a man face to face on request, and you feel how weightless the demand was.

**"Verily, He is Most High, Most Wise."** Ibn Kathir glosses this closing of ayah 51: "He is Most High, All-Knowing, Most Wise." Sit with how the two names answer the two halves of the ayah. He is *ʿAlī*, Most High — and one does not summon the Most High to an audience on human terms. And He is *Ḥakīm*, Most Wise — so the three channels He has chosen read not as a withholding but as a wisdom: contact delivered in exactly the way the creature can receive it.

## Ayah 52: "And thus We have sent to you Ruh of Our command"

"And thus" ties ayah 52 back to ayah 51: by this same practice, in these same ways, waḥy came to you, O Muhammad ﷺ. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the link explicit — this ayah is "a complement of the subject of the first verse." Its gist, in that commentary's summary: in this world nobody has ever seen, nor can ever see and converse face to face with Allah; however, Allah does send waḥy to His chosen servants in the three ways described in the first ayah, and in accordance with that practice waḥy is sent to the Prophet ﷺ as well.

What is the *Rūḥ* sent of Allah's command? Ibn Kathir answers in one word: **the Qur'an.**

**"You knew not what is the Book, nor what is Faith."** This phrase has to be handled carefully, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān handles it carefully. Ibn Kathir's gloss is that this means "in the details which were given to you in the Qur'an." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān expands: unawareness of the Book before waḥy is quite obvious; and "absence of knowledge of faith" means that faith's details, its rules and regulations, and its exalted place become known to a prophet *after* waḥy, not before it.

It does **not** mean he was without faith. On the contrary, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states that it is proved **with the consensus of the ummah** that whomever Allah chooses to make His Messenger or Prophet, He gives him faith and belief right from the beginning of his birth — "his faith is engraved in his nature." These chosen people are firm believers even before prophethood and before waḥy is sent to them; the principles of belief become a part of their nature and behaviour.

The commentary then offers a striking historical proof: all the prophets were opposed by their people, who piled up all sorts of allegations against them — **yet no one had ever accused a prophet of idolatry, even before he was appointed as a prophet.** Their enemies, who would have used anything against them, could not find that. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Qurtubi in his Tafsir, and Qadi ʿIyad in *Shifāʼ*, have dealt with this subject in full detail.

The deeper point of the sentence is a lesson in humility about knowledge itself. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, whatever knowledge a man obtains — even a prophet, for that matter — is all a grant of Allah. Ayah 52 makes even the Messenger ﷺ a recipient before he is a teacher.

## Light, and two kinds of guidance

"But We have made it a light wherewith We guide whosoever of Our servants We will." Ibn Kathir identifies "it" as the Qur'an, and pairs this with 41:44: *"Say: 'It is for those who believe, a guide and a healing. And as for those who disbelieve, there is heaviness (deafness) in their ears, and it (the Qur'an) is blindness for them.'"*

The same Book, two opposite effects. A light does not illuminate a closed eye. So the Qur'an is not a text that works mechanically on whoever opens it; it is light for the one Allah wills to guide, and the one who comes to it in refusal finds only heaviness and blindness.

Then the ayah turns to the Prophet ﷺ: **"And verily, you are indeed guiding to a straight path."** Ibn Kathir explains "you" as "O Muhammad," and "a straight path" here as *the correct behavior*. Hold this beside the clause just before it — *We* guide whosoever We will — and the two guidances sit side by side without conflict: the Prophet ﷺ guides by showing the road, calling and teaching; Allah alone guides by putting light in the heart that walks it.

## Ayah 53: whose path it is

Ibn Kathir observes that Allah then "explains this further" — ayah 53 refuses to leave "a straight path" as an abstraction and immediately identifies it: **"The path of Allah"** — which Ibn Kathir explains as **His Laws which He enjoins.** Not a vague spirituality, not a road each person maps for himself, but the concrete commands Allah has legislated.

And then the credentials of the One whose path it is: "to Whom belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is on the earth." Ibn Kathir: this means "their Lord and Sovereign, the One Who is controlling and ruling them, Whose decree cannot be overturned." This is why the path is binding. A route laid down by the Lord and Sovereign of the heavens and the earth is not one option among many.

The surah then closes: **"Verily, all matters at the end go to Allah."** Ibn Kathir: all matters come back to Him and He issues judgement concerning them — "Glorified and exalted be He far above all that the evildoers and deniers say."

That final clause is a fitting ending for the surah. The passage began with revelation coming *down* from Allah; it ends with every affair travelling *back* to Him. The objectors of ayah 51, who set the terms on which they would believe, are themselves a "matter" that returns to Allah for judgement.

## Living it

**Take the Book as light, not decoration.** If ayah 52 calls the Qur'an a *Rūḥ* sent of Allah's command, and a light by which He guides, then a heart that never sits with it is choosing to stay in the dark. And 41:44 warns that for those who do not believe there is heaviness in the ears and blindness; how you come to it decides what it does to you.

**Let the Ibn Hibban hadith govern your work.** Your provision and your term are both already complete measures. So neither panic nor idleness fits: *have Taqwa of Allah, and keep seeking in a good and lawful way.* Effort, yes — but lawful effort, without the fear that drives people into what Allah has forbidden.

**Rest the longing to see Him where it belongs.** The curtain in this world is the weakness of our vision, not His distance; and in Paradise, when that vision is strengthened, every dweller of Heaven will be favoured with the ability to see Allah. That reframes the whole of worship — you are not speaking into an absence, but to One who is *ʿAlī*, Most High, and *Ḥakīm*, Most Wise in exactly how much He lets you receive now.

**Treat the Sharia as the road, not the fence.** The straight path of ayah 53 is defined as the Laws Allah enjoins, laid down by the Lord and Sovereign of the heavens and the earth. When obedience feels heavy, ayah 53 gives the two facts that lighten it: it is *His* path, and to Him all matters at the end go.
